items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — The Basque culture that straddles the northeastern part of Spain and southwestern region of Francehas fascinated linguists and anthropologists alike owing to the fact that this culture appears to beone of the last remnants of Paleolithic Europe before the arrival of the Indo-Europeans. Given thisculture's rather isolate position in terms of its relationship amongst other European cultures, it'slittle wonder that it too has developed some of its own unique musical styles. While little known tothe outside world, the Basque region did indeed participate in the flavorful sounds that emergedduring the psychedelic and progressive years and thanks to DJ Makala who compiled a number of tracksfrom various artists, this excellent compilation is like a box of assorted chocolates awaiting yourdiscovery.KATEBEGIAK Prog-Rock, Psych-Folk & Jazz-Rock Music from the Basque Country was released in 2021 andhighly acclaimed for showcasing some of the region's history that was the crucial link thatconnected the folk revivalists of the 1960s and the Basque Radical Rock (Euskal Herriko rockerradikala) that fueled the regions punk scene. The term KATEBEGIAK actually means "Links of achain." The album features 13 select tracks that display the wide array of experimental sounds thatsprang up in the 1970s and continued into the 80s. After the 60s revival movement, bands began tocross-pollinate their homegrown folk music with the various forms of psychedelia, rock and jazzfusion that were springing up all around Europe and the world since the mid-1960s and this Whitman'ssample pack is the perfect place to dip in and get a taste of such sounds for further exploration.This release features all the expected artists such as the most popular Basque act Itoiz as well asHaizea, Enbor and Errobi but also features some of the rarest of the rare with bands such as thePamplona based Magdalena and the virtually unknown Urria. Strangely this collection features arather interesting choice of what to include and what not as it features the track "Pello Joxepe"which as an outlier from rest and features a Mississippi born black psychedelic soul singer coveringa traditional Basque song and yet the release doesn't include real Basque acts that existed at thetime including Sakre, Akelarre, Mirotz and Patxi Villamor. Track lengths vary considerably as wellranging from the 3 1/2 minute "Agurra II" from Enbor to the longest track "Andere" from Errobi whichsprawls out to 13 1/2 minutes. While these acts varied widely in approach, the thread that keeps it all connected is the softsensual folk and oft flute oriented music that in some ways resembles Celtic folk music but soundsas distinct as the language this unique population has kept alive despite all odds. Some of thetrack placements are a bit odd as the opening "Egunaren Hastapena" by Haizea takes a good fiveminutes to slowly work up to some sort of song structure. The following "Xori Bele" by Izkaitzwould've been a better choice as it provides a more direct introduction into the culturalsmorgasbord about to be experience however this is hardly a deal breaker as all the tracks areworthy of an attentive listen. While most of these artists are clearly more in the psychedelic folk camp with touches of prog rockin for the mix, bands like Lisker actually deliver the more rocking bravado whereas the tracks byAmala Zubrina & Pascual Gaigne along with the album's closer by Urria are extremely ethereal and themost experimental. Despite the urge to play these in a different order it's the music that countsand although i've heard of many of these bands i haven't actually heard them so this is the perfectway to get acquainted as well as finding some rarities that have completely escaped the attention ofeven the most sleuth oriented databases. The Basque scene was quite distinct from the Rock Andaluzand jazz fusion scenes of the rest of Spain and this compilation is the perfect way to explore thisoften neglected region of the nation. Pretty much every track works for me however i wish theexcluded acts were on this one too.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张收录巴斯克地区1972-1985年间实验摇滚、迷幻民谣与爵士摇滚融合作品的合辑。专辑展现了巴斯克文化独特的音乐遗产，将本土民谣传统与欧洲前卫摇滚、爵士融合元素相结合。曲目从三分钟的短作到十三分钟的长篇均有涉及，体现了当时音乐实验的多样性。评论者强调该合辑作为探索巴斯克地下音乐世界的窗口价值，涵盖了从知名乐团Itoiz、Haizea到近乎未知的小众乐队。虽然评论指出曲目编排偶有突兀之处，但这张独立发行的选集成功呈现了该地区在前卫与实验音乐领域的文化独特性，对于关注世界音乐与实验融合的听众具有探索价值。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — After delivering a fairly unadulterated slice of traditional Basque folk music on its debut, HAIZEAjoined the late 70s craze of incorporating elements of 70s prog and 60s psychedelia into its mix andin the process took a huge leap with a substantially more adventurous and explorative sophomorerelease. On HONTZ GAUA which is Basque for "Night of the Owl," guitarist / vocalist Txomin Artolaleft the group in pursuit of a solo career and in his place flautist and guitarist Xabier Iriondojoined the ranks and helped usher HAIZEA into much more progressive territories with its set of fivetracks that only added up to just over 33 minutes. A much more avant-garde album, HONTZ GAUA wasbuilt around the same traditional Basque folk melodies of the debut only embellished with moreethereal atmospheric effects, less rigid compositional structures and extended excursions that wereinspired by the European progressive rock of the 1970s.The opening track belies the album's ambitious nature with a rather tame traditional approach."Anderea" sounds like a leftover from the previous album but starting with the second track"Egunaren Hastapena" the band blossoms quite quickly into a darker tone with less predictable songstructures all the while the feminine charm of Amala Zubira takes on a darker at times even gothicapproach sounding something like if Sandy Denny was auditioning for Dead Can Dance. Althoughprimarily acoustic in nature, electric guitars are used more liberally this time around withpsychedelic dressing applied to tracks like "Argizagi Ederra" to great affect as well asincorporating more demanding time signature approaches rather than untempered guitar chordstrumming. Irondo adds a lot of intricate flute moments as well as adding the distinguished tones ofthe Portuguese guitar. "Arnaki" offers a twin guitar effect which takes the music into a 60spsychedelic vibe.Once again all lyrics are in the Basque language which offers a unique rhythmic flow unlike any ofthe Romance languages and therefore sounds quite distinct from the Rock Andaluz acts that wereflooding Spain in the 70s. Touches of jazz are incorporated for musical textures but nothing in thefusion sense ever intrudes on the rather subdued psychedelic light-hearted nature of the album evenwhen the twin electric guitars are at the most feisty. The jewel in the crown is the side long titletrack broken down into two distinct segments which at over 14 minutes offer plenty of excursionsinto true unrestricted progressive territories. Beginning with a Gregorian chant followed by abaptizing water sound effect sequence before gently rolling out the flute and acoustic guitar beforethe ethereal vocal harmonies kick in. Tender percussion is added and the track oozes around quicklyskillfully as it shape shifts through various musical motifs steeped in heavy psychedelic effectswith some sort of chimes and intricate changes through varying passages. Easily the best track ofthe band's career.The light airy feel of the album laced with beautiful melodies and adventurous performances in anexotic language may make you feel like you've drifted away into some far away land as HAIZEAaugments its Basque folk traditions into powerful psychedelic folk statements. Laced withtraditional wind instruments and various percussive techniques, HONTZ GAUA adds a sense of darknessliving up to its title meaning of "Night of the Owl." Zubiria delivers an excellent display of vocalcontrol evolving beyond her cutsie good girl folk style of the debut and the icing on the cake arethe explorative shifts in song structure that feel organically natural and not hastily thrown intothe mix. A guest violinist delivers some serous melancholy and band displayed a remarkable maturityon this sophomore offering most likely due to the fact much time was spent the previous yearsbetween albums on the live circuit and best of all the band seriously integrated the progcharacteristics perfectly. A charming mellow album that is one of the highlights of the Basqueinfused prog folk craze of the era.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张1979年的巴斯克进步民谣专辑，在传统巴斯克民谣基础上融入了70年代前卫摇滚与60年代迷幻元素。专辑仅收录五首曲目约33分钟，其中14分钟的同名标题曲尤为突出，包含格里高利圣咏、水声采样、长笛与声乐和声，并通过丰富的迷幻效果实现多变的音乐转变。乐评指出乐队虽仍以原声乐器为主，但电吉他与爵士元素的使用使音乐更具实验性，双吉他编排带来60年代迷幻氛围，人声部分有时呈现暗黑甚至哥特式的质感。全部巴斯克语歌词赋予了音乐独特的韵律感，与当时西班牙的Rock Andaluz风格形成鲜明对比。对于偏好实验与前卫音乐的听众而言，这张融合传统民谣与进步摇滚的小众作品具有较高的探索价值。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The third and final part of Gong's Radio Gnome Invisible trilogy, where Zero, the hero, receives his cosmic ascension, activating his third eye...deserved an imposing musical framework, befitting the importance of the events narrated. This volume thus became the most musically daring, the most experimental, and the one with the longest tracks. While each part was unique in its own way...and Angel's Egg had innovated with the short duration of its tracks and yet all its stylistic variety, You further developed these concepts, taking them a step further and becoming a classic not only for the band but for the genre itself.As the cover promises...there's a mix of spacey atmosphere and indigenous mysticism in Thoughts for Naught, Daevid Allen's composition, his ability to draw the rest into his universe...Tim Blake's synthesizers and Mike Howlett's bass in Magick Mother Invocation, creating that spacey psychedelia that always starts slowly...Didier Malherbe's saxophone, Gilli Smyth's vocals, and of course Pierre and Beno�t Moerlen's drums and percussion...plus Steve Hillage's ineffable and unmistakable guitar...everything will conspire to make that conjunction of stars explode in this volume.Master Builder is the construction of that curtain of synthesizers and the Buddhist choir...the percussion, the flute in an oriental orchestra...until the drums introduce the saxophone and the space rock jam...the cosmic French psychedelic free jazz begins...you can smell the 70s...you can feel it...there is precision, there is technique...yes...but there is also madness, freedom, anarchy, bohemianism, and that mix is ​​what made this Gong so special, ultimately, Allen's invocatory presence. When Hillage begins to play...nobody was prepared for that cascade of sound...for those doors that open in the mind with the notes of his sound...which, supported by the synthesizer, the drums and the bass, will make history.You is an album that wasn't rushed...in a decade that seized control of time to do with it as it saw fit for artistic purposes...and if this meant accelerating it to the point of confusion like King Crimson on Red...or slowing it down to the point of despair...like Gentle Giant on Free Hand...there was no doubt they were going to do it, and Gong took the time to build each step of ascent on You...because they knew that the feeling of climbing step by step is not the same as skipping steps in pursuit of a rush that only speaks of detachment from things.As layers of synthesizers build upon the drums in A Sprinkling of Clouds, and the drums with each hit seem to leap from the speakers and reach us as only a few records can...and the guitar sounds wild yet clean at the same time and you can follow its path at every moment...when Didier Malherbe joins in we understand why they distanced themselves from anyone who could do something similar and Frank Zappa's Inca's Roads didn't end up going in the same direction either.Perfect Mystery revisits the cabaret atmosphere of Angel's Egg only as a connection within the story, that oriental atmosphere that sets the stage for The Isle of Everywhere, one of the album's central themes...where synthesizers, Gilli Smyth's vocals, bass, and drums create an atmosphere reminiscent of King Crimson's Islands...only to then turn around and take another route, because Mike Howlett's swing on the bass had the necessary propulsion to soar without sopranos...and Gong sometimes has the ability to pass the third eye to us, if we can connect with his music; it's jazz...it's progressive rock...it's funk...it's psychedelia...it's the Canterbury scene, born in part because an Australian couldn't return to England and had to stay in France.Steve Hillage's solo begins so subtly behind the saxophone...but it does define itself throughout the entire development, supported by the bass and drums, at times playing with parts of jazz rock, until You Never Blow Your Trip Forever encompasses everything heard so far in the trilogy, even more psychedelic if possible...until it settles as if unintentionally into a section that, from improvised and played, culminates in another inspired song/prayer to the universe...a mantra repeated and destined to fade away, the complete opposite of this third volume of the most classic Gong which, as if it were a loop in time...must be repeated again and again once it has already ended.
items._cn_summary: GONG《You》作为1974年坎特伯雷场景的标志性作品，将空间迷幻、东方神秘主义与自由爵士即兴融为一体，是一张高度实验性的前卫摇滚专辑。Steve Hillage的吉他与Tim Blake合成器构建出层层叠加的声响空间，Didier Malherbe的萨克斯将法式迷幻爵士推向极致，佛教合唱与东方管弦乐元素则增添了独特的文化底蕴。专辑的长时间曲目与渐进式结构展现了创作者对时间的精准把控，体现了七十年代前卫摇滚对艺术性的执着追求。对于偏好实验与即兴风格的用户而言，这张专辑提供了丰富的聆听细节与跨类型融合的典范。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As if a metronome were forcing its angle further and further outwards...expanding the range until it distorted...the trio, which didn't evoke the image of a trio, begins its second album with "A Visit to Newport Hospital," showcasing organ variations that sound like alarms, red alerts...Dave Stewart combines the magic of the 60s with the mysterious psychedelia that in the 70s would give way to that other Canterbury metric, and Mont Campbell with his measured vocals, plus the organ overlays from which the guiding threads would emerge, the solos of that melody which, as promised at the beginning, were nothing more than alarms of variation on the same note. Jazz and Bossa Nova are implicitly present...staining like raindrops on petals. The alarm awakens us.Contrasong features two tenor saxophones and two trumpets...the monotonous rhythm goes hand in hand with Mont Campbell's singing, and that piano that cuts through Clive Brooks' drums...which cuts through the trumpets...and cuts through the saxophones...and suddenly we're in uncharted territory...like that cover that looks like molten lead, whose solidifying shapes were once used to predict the future... where the trio that did not evoke the image of a trio preferred the mystery of the promise of what it suggests...but is not seen, what is, but is not yet known...an eternal advance, which postpones its realization with the concrete certainty of something that can be heard...can be felt...but not touched, and that when trying to understand it moves away, and comes closer if the mode of perception changes.Boilk is more variations, but in reverse...another way of confirming that intellectual understanding only sets us back...is by not understanding the proposed rules...which are reminiscent of Gy�rgy Ligeti and works like Atmospheres. When, in the final coda, Stewart's other great passion emerges with the Baroque religious organ.Long Piece No. 3 is the album's centerpiece, and here Bach's counterpoints become progressive, slicing through space until they become silence, and then a floating, sidereal space sustained by the drums. Here the trio plays at being a quartet, with the organ's bass lines, leading to an even more ethereal section with the piano...where, from atonal, they could become aggressive, provocative, but always maintaining the tension, that mystery of not knowing what will come next...what note, what chord awaits around the return of the nebula.The second part continues with the variations, the key to the album, creating spacey atmospheres...where that molten lead seems to solidify and take shape...but new suspended melodies, which distanced them from other bands of the genre, anchor them with that Hammond organ with one foot in the 60s, the same as Pink Floyd's Atom Heart Mother, but firm to the pattern that it is the organ that leads the race, this race without a visible final objective.The third part is considered the most complex, alternating between keyboard and piano, with the piano sections being the most virtuosic and classically accomplished. At times, it recalls the darker segments of Emerson, Lake & Palmer's Pictures at an Exhibition.The fourth and final part is even faster, related to Soft Machine's debut, but the jazzy Bossa rhythm with the keyboard cuts and repetitions, plus the bass and the out-of-tune keyboard, end up distancing it and solidifying this experiment of variations as the triumph of melodic harmony in all its forms.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张1971年英国Canterbury Scene的经典专辑，由Egg三人乐团呈现。乐评展现了实验性、先锋性的音乐特质，融合了爵士即兴、Bossa Nova节奏、巴洛克复调音乐以及现代古典元素（如Ligeti的氛围音乐概念）。评论详细描述了乐队如何打破传统三重奏框架，通过organ与piano的交织创造空间感，以及Dave Stewart对Baroque宗教音乐的运用。Long Piece No.3作为核心作品，将Bach式赋格转化为前卫探索，展现了从调性到无调性的动态张力。该专辑与Pink Floyd《Atom Heart Mother》同处一个时代，但更倾向于实验而非流行表达。整体而言，这是一部高度创新、跨越爵士-古典-实验边界的作品，与用户的实验/前卫及现代作曲口味高度吻合。

items.album: Ivan Pavlov interview: ‘The book is the final Soisong release’
items.excerpt: Ivan Pavlov, who records as CoH, co-founded Soisong with the late Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson in Bangkok in 2007. The project produced the octagonal “Soisong EP” tour CDEP in 2008 and the full-length “xAj3z,” which documented two European tours. The project held its final concert at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010 – without Christopherson, whose health had declined to the point that he could not fly. Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010.
items.body: Ivan Pavlov, who records as CoH, co-founded Soisong with the late Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson in Bangkok in 2007. The project produced the octagonal “Soisong EP” tour CDEP in 2008 and the full-length “xAj3z,” which documented two European tours. The project held its final concert at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010 – without Christopherson, whose health had declined to the point that he could not fly. Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010. A 2012 event at Bar Bonobo in Tokyo, the venue where the project’s first concert had taken place, marked a symbolic close. On May 22, 2026, Pavlov released “Soisong Book” – a 160-page faux-leather hardcover limited to 222 numbered copies – through the official Soisong store. The book draws on email correspondence, private photographs, official announcements, manifestos, and items Pavlov describes as “fake documents”: promotional materials created during the project’s active years. Two CDs are affixed inside the cover: a 2007 Tokyo concert recording pre-dating Soisong’s formation, and a new studio album by trumpet player Julio Ecclesiast, who contributed to “xAj3z.” Side-Line spoke with Pavlov about the archive behind the book, the nature of some of Soisong’s listed performers, the night in Berlin, and what follows this release. Soisong interview SL: The book draws heavily on email exchanges between you and Sleazy. How large was that archive, and what guided your selection process? Were there exchanges you wanted to include but felt were too private? Ivan Pavlov: I have about a thousand emails in my mailbox filed under ‘Sleazy’, but since it’s a Soisong book, only those that relate to the process have been included. SL: You described upscaling late-2000s cellphone photos and low-res Myspace images using current technology. Where did you draw the line between restoring what was there and altering it? Did any images come out looking wrong once upscaled? Ivan Pavlov: Good upscaling algorithms do not alter images to anything one would be able to notice in print, so no, the printed images look the same as their low-res originals. SL: The book includes what you describe as “fake documents.” Can you give a specific example – were these created during the project’s active years, or produced later for the book? Ivan Pavlov: You can see them in the book. For example, as part of the campaign for Soisong album called ‘xAj3z’ we had published a so-called Report from an, obviously non-existent, Investigating Committee. The report speculated on and promoted the shape of the CD package as an extraterrestrial object, with multiple illustrations. This was all made back in 2009. SL: 222 copies is a precise figure. Is there a reason for that specific number, or was it determined by print-run economics? Ivan Pavlov: You may find in the book a rather extensive dialogue about choosing the name for the project. I won’t expand too much on that, but ‘song’ is ‘two’ in Thai language. As for the economics for any kind of small editions – it is tough, indeed. SL: The first CD captures the 2007 Tokyo concert where CoH and The Threshold House Boys Choir performed as separate acts – a pre-Soisong moment. Why that recording specifically? Was it already in the archive, or did it require sourcing? Ivan Pavlov: Back then, a few days after the show I received 2 CDs from the sound engineer who was at the main desk during the concert. One with a room recording, i.e. including the sound of the audience, one with the clean signal. I now made a mix of the two and I see it as a document well related to Soisong – in the book you will find a mention of the show, and the subsequent discussion on playing live. SL: The second CD contains a new studio album by Julio Ecclesiast, the trumpet player from “xAj3z.” How did that collaboration come about – did you approach him, or did the idea come from him? How much input did you have in the direction of his album? Ivan Pavlov: Just like several other participants in Soisong, Julio mostly exists in domains of imagination, listener’s imagination included. Which already back in 2009 had become a rather typical, important part of Soisong’s approach to choosing the performers. SL: Soisong’s packaging choices were consistently unusual – the octagonal CDEP, the warning on “xAj3z” that it could only play in CD players with a flat horizontal tray. How much of that approach came from Sleazy, and how much from you? Ivan Pavlov: I would usually come up with rough geometrical design ideas, which we then perfected through a mutually encouraging dialogue. SL: The final Soisong show took place at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010, without Sleazy. What do you remember about that night, and what was the decision behind going ahead without him? Ivan Pavlov: There was no decision making as such, as far as I remember we were about to play a few shows in Europe, but then Sleazy’s health suddenly declined which didn’t let him fly. The show in Berlin was too late to cancel, so we went on with this kind of ‘remote version’. Sleazy recorded a video message to the audience, and a video stream for me to play during the show. I played the music. It felt quite lonely on the stage, I admit. SL: Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010 – the city where Soisong was based. How did you decide what to do with the project’s archive after that? Was there a point where you considered closing it entirely? Ivan Pavlov: Soisong is pretty much closed ever since Sleazy’s departure. Whatever has been published afterwards – these are just echoes of the past on their way to the future. Soisong was only meant to last until 2012, so in 2012 we organised the symbolic final event at Bar Bonobo, in Tokyo. That’s where Soisong played the very first concert, commonly referred to as Test Run #7. During this final night at Bonobo in 2012, with the help of the bar’s owner Koichi Sei and a few other friends, the recording of Test Run #7 was released in a small edition of sealed Walkman CD players. Some years later, I also managed to put together the unfinished Soisong album ‘kAm1e’. Now comes the book, which is pretty much just a collection of artefacts. I believe we would have published this kind of the final statement if Sleazy was alive, too. SL: Dais Records released a remastered deluxe 2LP of “xAj3z” in 2025, with one previously unreleased track, “Lom Tum Lai Kwee.” How did that reissue come about, and what was it like returning to that material? Ivan Pavlov: Dais expressed interest in re-issuing the two Soisong releases on vinyl. I wouldn’t have been able to pull that off on my own, and the idea seemed attractive. So I agreed and we did it. As for coming back to Soisong material – be it email conversations, images or music – it always feels warm, feels like coming home. SL: You said the book’s creation was fuelled by “the same joyful enthusiasm and sense of fun as every other publication.” How would you describe Soisong’s working method to someone who only knows the music? Ivan Pavlov: Encouraging joyful enthusiasm in each other, and working with a sense of common fun – that is the only method we employed. SL: Does “Soisong Book” function as a closing document, or is there still archive material that could surface in future releases? Ivan Pavlov: The book is the final Soisong release. I might do a few more commemorative fake radio-broadcasts for soisong.bandcamp.com. I would also definitely like to work more with Julio Ecclesiast, which largely depends on how he feels about that… but officially as Soisong, there are no further releases planned. Soisong Broadcast #13 by SOISONG About Soisong Soisong was an experimental electronic music project formed in 2007 by Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson and Ivan Pavlov (CoH), based in Bangkok, Thailand. Christopherson had previously worked with Throbbing Gristle, Psychic TV, Coil, and The Threshold Houseboys Choir, while Pavlov released music under the CoH name. The project combined Pavlov’s computer-based composition with Christopherson’s work on artificial vocals and what the project described as “South Seas” instrumentation. The first release, “Soisong EP,” was an octagonal tour CDEP issued in 2008 in disposable-design packaging, with the release title doubling as a password for additional material on the project’s website. The full-length “xAj3z” followed, in octagonal packaging and carrying a warning that the disc could only play in CD players with a flat horizontal tray. Live activity included the 2008 Test Run Tour – with dates in Tokyo, Rovereto, Copenhagen, Bilbao, Amsterdam, Moscow, and Athens – and a 2009 reunion tour with shows in Linz, Moscow, St. Petersburg, Wroclaw, and Cologne. The final concert took place at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010, performed without Christopherson. Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010. A 2012 event at Bar Bonobo in Tokyo, site of the project’s first concert, served as a symbolic close: the recording of that original Tokyo show, Test Run #7, was issued in a small edition of sealed Walkman CD players. Pavlov subsequently assembled the unfinished album “kAm1e.” Dais Records reissued “xAj3z” as a remastered deluxe 2LP in 2025, with the previously unreleased track “Lom Tum Lai Kwee” added to the Bandcamp edition released on May 30, 2025. “Soisong Book,” released May 22, 2026, is confirmed as the final Soisong release.
items._cn_summary: Soisong是由CoH主脑Ivan Pavlov与Throbbing Gristle传奇成员Peter Christopherson于2007年在曼谷共同创立的实验音乐项目。该书籍《Soisong Book》以档案形式呈现，包含邮件往来、私人照片及项目方自称的“假文件”，并限量发行222份，内含两张CD——一张是2007年东京演出录音，另一张是与xAj3z专辑相关的 trumpet player Julio Ecclesiast新专辑。整本书通过原始邮件、演出记录和虚构文件交织，呈现出一种独特的文献式艺术手法。这篇文章为访谈形式，深入探讨了项目背景、图像修复技术和创作意图。对于偏好实验与暗潮的用户而言，Soisong本身即为该领域的标志性项目，而书籍的出版形式更强化了其跨媒介的实验性与文献收藏价值。

items.body: We have Vancouver’s own Verboden Festival coming up this weekend in our backyard, and we’re excited about seeing a slew of familiar faves like SRSQ and Male Tears as well as catching acts we’ve been tracking through studio material but have yet to catch live, like Dildox and More Ephemerol. Hope to catch up with regular readers/listeners, too – should be a great weekend. On with this week’s tracks! Scimitar Street Sects, “No Percentage In Caution” The pair of LPs released by long-standing industrial punk terrorists Street Sects gave us a lot to chew on last year, and the band’s declaration that they’re moving in a “more rhythm based/song focused direction” with their new stuff is intriguing. This first sample clearly finds some of the harmonic and synth hook elements of the Full Color Eclipse second being drawn into a rhythmically tight package. No Percentage in Caution by Street Sects Sydney Valette, “I Fucking Love You” We’ve come to associate Sydney Valette with a more continental and very French take on modern darkwave, avoiding many of the cliches of the style in favour of something that feels both classic, but without being beholden to the ur sources of the sound. New single “I Fucking Love You” holds with that, but sounds more strident than any of Valette’s work in recent memory. Partly it’s the tempo and push of the song, but also it’s a distinctly wounded and gothic vocal delivery, bringing out the emotion and drama here. If this is the direction of the new record, it could signal a nice shift into a new direction that would certainly be of interest to us as fans and followers of his work. I Fucking Love You by Sydney Valette Ortrotasce, “As I See It” Ortrotasce always keeps you on your toes; from single to single and within the run-time of the occasional longer release the one-man project deigns to release you’re never exactly sure where in the sprawling fields of synthpop, EBM, darkwave, and new beat things might land. You even have to keep your head on a pivot mid-track, as the peppy, Kraftwerkian programming of this early electro number is swiftly offset by a gloomy and resigned vocal which feels wholly separate. As I See It by Ortrotasce Transmigration, “Understanding” Last we checked in with the UK’s Transmigration, we noted their capacity to make the kind of gritty dark electro that benefits from obscurity and rough edges. New cut “Understanding”, the first taster from EP Living Information isn’t a huge leap away from that aesthetic, but it’s also a lot sharper and more direct, with atmosphere evolving out of the vocals, the speedy sequences and the aggression of the delivery, almost as a byproduct. The result is one of urgency, with a lot of the power stemming from how open and direct it all is, creating a sound that doesn’t need to be dressed up at all, arriving unforced, unadorned and hard-hitting. Living Information by Transmigration Scimitar, “Zenith (Inhalt remix)” Little bit of a ID:UD twofer this week with this Scimitar remix by Inhalt. We’ll be seeing the Los Angeles based band for the first time at Verboden this coming weekend, and we’re quite keen to do so; as an act we’ve tracked for a few years, they’ve consistently put out material that defies a lot of dark alt music trends, capturing sounds that are spiky, punky and uncompromising. And (spoilers) this week’s episode of We Have a Technical has Matia Simnovich of Inhalt as a guest, talking about the art of being a producer and what that entails. Tune into the latter, and then next week to hear our impressions of the performance from the former! Zenith (Inhalt Remix) by Scimitar Nikonn feat. MeLLLo, “Lighthouse” Lastly, something fairly off-format for us but still salient to our coverage. MeLLLo, AKA Marianthi Melitsi of the on-hiatus but never far from our playlists synthpop act Marsheaux, makes a guest vocal appearance on the new single by London producer Nikonn, and her familiar, soothing tone glides perfectly over this downtempo mix of dreampop and chillout instrumentation, making us wistful for the sorts of crepuscular ballads which complemented Marsheaux’s club numbers so very nicely. items.body: Ard Bit is the project of Norwegian Ard Janssen. The new album is called Juxtaposed , forty two minutes of intentional electronic soundscape, with muted pastel colors, nine tracks ranging from two to seven minutes. Similar to Biosphere, it's ambient, downtempo in bite-sized pieces, with nostalgic melodies, warm tones, lush pads, and clouds. Largely synth, but filled out with field recordings that crackle and sputter as air hits the microphone. Minor key atmospheres befitting dub techno are presented without drums, expansive reverberation extending out to the horizon. These are analog sound sources with the precision stereofield and clear mix that comes with digital arrangement. Sometimes it's just textured, tonally imbued air, and sometimes there's a clearer melody, sometimes played on a piano, in the case of closer "Fanal Magic". There are nods to traditional arpeggio-based synthesiser ambient on tracks like "Always Now", and a general sense of tunefulness. Fans of Boards of Canada should enjoy the gently saturated tape fidelity. In a track like "Silver Torch", tiny clicks and pops become implied drums. It is kind of deconstructed dance music in a similar fashion to Vladislav Delay. All in all, it's very inviting and expertly produced. The texture of the recording is like a massage. Each sound is perfectly treated. It tends to make one comfortable as the minutes pass. What more could you want? An album that should please both the soundscape connoisseur and the casual fan of chillout electronic.
items._cn_summary: Ard Bit是挪威音乐人Ard Janssen的氛围电子个人项目。《Juxtaposed》全长42分钟，涵盖9首2至7分钟的曲目，呈现出类似Biosphere和Boards of Canada的复古电子氛围美学。音乐以合成器垫音为核心，融合环境录音的细微声响（小破裂声、麦克风声），在模拟音色与数字精确混音之间取得平衡。部分曲目如“Always Now”借鉴传统合成器氛围乐的琶音手法，“Silver Torch”则以微小点击声暗示解构的节拍，类似Vladislav Delay的处理方式。专辑整体偏向无鼓小调氛围，虽缺乏爵士或世界音乐的跨界元素，但作为独立发行的电子氛围作品，其制作精良、声响处理细腻的特点，对于偏好实验电子和环境音景的听众具有较高吸引力。

items.body: Are you ready to embark on a sonic adventure? Travelogue [Thailand] is the third in an ongoing series from the Touch imprint, in which two artists meet in a designated location and record an audio diary of their experience: first Nepal, then Bali and now Thailand. Over the course of nine days, CM von Hausswolff & Chandra Shukla visited multiple locations in Chaing Mai, from hotels to museums to temples, ending their journey in the Lanna Kingdom (Kingdom of a million rice fields) recording rivers, forests, monasteries and tribes. Sculpting all of these sonic treasures into four distinct pieces, the artists now present a portrait of Thailand in all its richness: miraculous, mysterious and multi-layered. “Nók Bpàa” eases the listener into the album with the overlapping sounds of the forest, traffic and a swiftly rising drone. A sudden rush – a motor? – interrupts the placidity. The artists admit that their diaries are not always calm, but contain “noise laden cacophony.” This uncertainty keeps the listener alert for the next sonic shift or juxtaposition: temple bells and monkeys, machinery and macaws. In this dense tapestry, alluring sounds emerge from the fog, only to be re-subsumed. In contrast, “Naga” leaps out of the speakers with rushing water and ceremonial song. One would have preferred a bit more rounding off at the start, but the piece soon becomes a study of dynamic contrast, falling into silence before introducing ripple, chirp and drone. The human element is far more apparent, children chattering, adults conversing, bells ringing, all folded into a backdrop of water and reverberation. Is this the real Thailand, or the sonic equivalent of “everything, everywhere, all at once?” The answer is somewhere in-between, as the album exudes a (pleasant) feeling of sensory overload. “Muaythai Changmai” begins with what sounds like a street festival, an expression of exuberance. Soon one encounters the sounds of the marketplace: loudspeaker announcements and a raucous crowd milling around. The introduction of English is startling, but momentary. A band begins to play, interrupted by another musician whose instrument sounds like bagpipes. Percussion cuts through the noise, then stops as the previous sound re-emerges. This is cacophony. Listening is like moving through the streets, drinking it all in. Balance is temporarily restored by the chants that begin “Wai Phra Kao Wat,” as spirituality is integral to any study of Thailand; for a few minutes, the album sounds like its cover. The temple gongs are no longer in the background, but in the fore. This piece deepens one’s appreciation of all that has come before, and its position as the closing track is wise. After all of the travels and the whirlwind of experiences, it is time to slow down and reflect. The forest sounds return, and the sense of peace is restored. (Richard Allen)
items._cn_summary: 专辑《Travelogue [Thailand]》是CM von Hausswolff与Chandra Shukla在泰国清迈历经九天录制的声音旅行日记，以四段声音景观呈现这座城市的多元声场。音乐融合环境录音与实验电子手法，将寺庙钟声、市场喧嚣、森林虫鸣、河流水声等素材进行拼贴与叠加，构建出层次丰富且具沉浸感的声音空间。整张专辑充满动态对比与感官刺激，从开篇的森林与交通音景到中段充满祭仪感的水声与人声，再到结尾市场节庆的喧闹与寺庙吟诵，展示了泰国文化中日常与神圣并存的特质。作为Touch厂牌发行的独立实验作品，其声音艺术视角与田野录音的实验性手法高度契合用户的实验/前卫与世界音乐偏好。

items.body: Operating as Simon Pyke (aka Freeform) and various collaborative ventures, unveils Drift Works—twelve fractured post-ambient sketches unfolding in slow, seamless disintegration. A fluid, absorbing whole Operating as Simon Pyke (aka Freeform) and various collaborative ventures, unveils Drift Works—twelve fractured post-ambient sketches unfolding in slow, seamless disintegration. Across this aptly named collection, vaporous textures and instrumental detail drift through weightless atmospheres and luminous tonal flourishes. “Wall of Bagpipes” gathers harmonized drones into a hypnotic swell, while “Shoom Drone” glides through ghostly modulations that evoke faded memory and soft sensory haze—perhaps even some treated whispering elements pierce through, almost translucent in its projection. “Metatones” also unfurls brittle instrumental horns and delicate vocal textures that feel both distant and deeply intimate, floating miles above the surface in a haze of serene orchestration. Within these carefully threaded layers of motion and color, Pyke leans away from his typically brittle electronic terrain toward something warmer, more meditative. “Rise of Superfingers” radiates quiet uplift; “Mindkeys” taps out rhythmic clusters with restrained precision; “Maximum Monk” carries a suspended choral pulse; “Chime and Twinkly” unfurls delicate melodic strands that feel half-remembered, surfacing from somewhere distant and internal. Closing piece “Traut One” cascades with kaleidoscopic piano figures, bringing gentle resolution to a record that places Pyke in singular territory—shaping drifting sonic forms from machinery, ambience, and instrumental fragments into a fluid, absorbing whole. Drift Works is available on Bandcamp. Drift Works by Simon Pyke
items._cn_summary: Simon Pyke以Freeform之名发布的这张独立专辑，呈现十二首碎片化的后氛围音景。作品在缓慢的消解过程中展开，融合蒸汽般的音色纹理、幽灵化的调制音效以及处理过的低语元素，营造出失重的大气层与柔和的感官雾霭。专辑突破了其以往干脆的电子地形，转向更温暖、更冥想的声音质地，涵盖催眠的谐波 drones、克制的节奏群、悬浮的合唱脉冲以及半遗忘的纤细旋律线条。作为独立发行的实验电子作品，该专辑深度契合实验/前卫与电子音乐偏好，同时带有当代古典与暗潮音色的跨界特征，在器乐碎片与氛围机械的交织中塑造出流动而沉浸的整体音场。

items.body: Am Anfang war der Bass. Ayşe Hassan hat dem Power-Post-Punk der Savages um Jehnny Beth in den mittleren 2010ern mit ihrem Instrument jede Menge Dringlichkeit verpasst. Die ersten Sekunden von »Husbands« vergisst man ohnehin so leicht nicht mehr. Ihr erstes Soloalbum nimmt jetzt etwas den Druck raus. Als Esya nutzt sie kalte Maschinenmusik, Synthesizer und Drum Machines für einen Sound zwischen Industrial und Wave-Pop, versucht sich aber nicht an der unterkühlten Unnahbarkeit, die man hinter dem Mikro oft vermutet, sondern geht raus. Richtig raus. Das hat etwas Verletzliches, selbst dann, wenn Tracks wie »Heaven« pulsieren und sich beinahe überschlagen. Als Himmel bezeichnet sie hier die Clubs und Konzerthallen, deren Wände mehr Liebe und Hingabe gesehen haben als die meisten anderen. Auf Chasing Desire, für dessen sonnigen Keyboard-Beat Jessy Lanza verantwortlich zeichnet, wird sich Esya nicht ganz einig und singt insgesamt achtzehnmal »I (don’t) want to be your lover«. Was sie aber weiß und was dem Album sehr gut steht, ist der langsame Sog, der im Laufe der etwas über 30 Minuten entsteht. Die Drums verabschieden sich immer weiter in die zweite Reihe, was Highlights wie »Hiding Place« auf den Plan ruft, das im besten Sinne so klingt, als würde es die nächste Minimal-Wave-Compilation anführen.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由前Savages乐队成员Ayşe Hassan以Esya名义创作，融合了冷冽的机械音乐、合成器与鼓机音效，介于工业音乐与新浪潮流行之间。Jessy Lanza参与的阳光键盘节拍为作品增添了流畅感。整张专辑在约30分钟内逐渐展开，鼓点逐步退居背景，营造出缓慢而持续吸引力，亮点曲目如《Hiding Place》带有极简新浪潮合辑的气质。作品展现出工业美学与电子声响的跨界融合，同时保留了后朋克背景中的紧迫感与情感深度，整体风格与用户的暗潮、电子音乐偏好高度匹配，且具有独立音乐的实验性特质。

items.body: Over the past few years, Ukrainian artist Dronny Darko has become a familiar name within the Drone, Cinematic, and Dark-Ambient landscape. Better known under his alias Dronny Darko, one has to go back to 2012 to find his very first release. Since then, he has evolved into an exceptionally prolific artist, unveiling countless albums, including a wide range of collaborations. His sonic universe serves as a platform where darkness, introspection, and existential unrest take center stage. Dronny Darko’s latest album, “Dark Shadows Across A Disordered Mind”, released through Cryo Chamber, feels like an intense descent into the depths of a fractured mind: claustrophobic, emotionally charged, and at the same time hypnotically beautiful. With icy drones, distorted textures, and an almost Cinematic build-up of tension, he conjures an auditory nightmare that continues to resonate long after the final note has faded. As far as I am concerned, this is not only one of his darkest works to date, but perhaps also his most personal. What follows is the account of our conversation. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Dark Shadows Across a Disordered Mind by Dronny Darko Dronny Darko interview Q: As a Ukrainian artist, it feels only natural to begin by addressing the impact the war has had on you personally. To what extent has this situation influenced your music—perhaps even turning it into a form of emotional outlet? And what role have music and the act of creation come to play for you in times of war? Oleh: Sound has always been an essential part of my life—it’s not something that emerged in response to circumstances, but rather something constant that I return to regardless of what is happening around me. The war didn’t fundamentally change my relationship with sound, but it did influence my internal state. It introduced a certain weight, grounding me in a more immediate, physical reality. At times, it felt as though my perspective narrowed, becoming more focused and restrained. However, I see this not as a loss, but as a phase of recalibration. I’m currently working toward reconnecting with that broader, more intuitive ‘antenna’—that sense of openness and sensitivity that allows me to translate abstract emotional states into sound. Q: Since your first release in 2012, you have built an incredibly prolific body of work, including numerous collaborations. Where do you situate your latest album, “Dark Shadows Across A Disordered Mind”, within this extensive discography, and what were you aiming to express or achieve with this new opus? Oleh: Yes, there is a deeper personal connection in this work. While much of my previous material has been more focused on abstract or environmental landscapes, this album leans more into internal space. Perhaps aside from “Outer Tehom”, this is one of the few releases where inner emotional states played a more direct role in shaping the sound. Current events inevitably left their imprint, and for once, I felt compelled to express something more introspective. Still, I tend to avoid over-defining these inner worlds—the listener should have space to interpret and experience them individually. Q: The album title suggests something deeply introspective and psychologically charged. What is the underlying meaning behind it, and how closely is it connected to your own inner state during the composition process? Oleh: Yes, there is a deeper personal connection in this work. While much of my previous material has been more focused on abstract or environmental landscapes, this album leans more into internal space. Perhaps aside from “Outer Tehom”, this is one of the few releases where inner emotional states played a more direct role in shaping the sound. Current events inevitably left their imprint, and for once, I felt compelled to express something more introspective. Still, I tend to avoid over-defining these inner worlds—the listener should have space to interpret and experience them individually. Q: To my ears, “Dark Shadows Across A Disordered Mind” feels like one of your darkest—if not the darkest—albums to date. How do you perceive this yourself, and how strongly is the atmosphere tied to the themes you explore? Oleh: I believe the title reflects the sonic character of the album quite accurately. To me, it evokes the sensation of moving through an empty hospital corridor—sterile, quiet, yet charged with an underlying tension. Every small sound becomes amplified in that environment. There’s a sense of systems being overloaded, of something not functioning as it should, and that creates a kind of internal disorientation. The music mirrors that feeling: subtle, restrained, but constantly on the edge of unraveling. Q: Did this album mark any significant evolutions or innovations in your creative process or sound? More broadly, how does the transition from one release to the next unfold for you? To what extent does innovation play a role—whether in terms of concept, thematic focus, or the use of new techniques and instruments? Oleh: With each new album, I try to introduce some form of evolution—whether subtle or more pronounced. Experimentation is a core part of why I continue creating. For this release, I was particularly interested in working with tape-based processes. I had been wanting to explore that medium for some time, and conceptually, this project felt like the right space to do so. Tape introduces its own imperfections and textures, which aligned naturally with the themes of distortion, memory, and psychological fragmentation present in the album. Q: You have collaborated with a wide range of artists over the years. What do you seek in a collaboration that differs from your solo work? And, picking up on the idea of evolution, are there specific collaborators who have pushed you artistically in new directions? Oleh: Collaboration offers a completely different creative dynamic. It allows you to observe how another artist thinks, how they approach sound, and what techniques they rely on. For a collaboration to be meaningful, there needs to be a sense of complementarity—if both artists are doing the same thing, there’s little room for growth. I tend to gravitate toward working with people who challenge me, often those I perceive as more skilled or experienced in certain areas. It’s less about being ‘pushed’ in a direct sense, and more about a mutual shaping of each other’s sonic environments. Through that interaction, new directions emerge naturally. Q: I imagine you are already working on new material. Can you share anything about what’s ahead, and what other plans you have for the remainder of the year? Oleh: At the moment, I’m working on a collaboration with my wife, Sasha, under her project ProtoU. This material is quite different from my usual work—we’re focusing more on acoustic elements and organic sound sources. The thematic direction is centered around Ukraine, which brings a different kind of emotional and cultural depth to the project. We’ve also recently connected with a craftsman and musician who builds and plays traditional ethnic instruments. He shared a range of recordings with us, and we’re now in the process of integrating these sounds into a cohesive musical narrative. It’s an ongoing exploration—figuring out how to shape these raw elements into something that feels both authentic and meaningful.

items.body: Flemish trio Kregel was formed in 2016 and began releasing EPs in 2020. In the meantime, the band has already arrived at “#7,” a new release featuring four fresh tracks. Kregel is quite a remarkable band because there are not many acts like them around. Musically, they are deeply rooted in the spirit of the 1980s, particularly the New-Wave and Post-Punk era. That alone is not unusual nowadays, but what truly makes the group stand out is their decision to sing in their native language while delivering wonderfully absurd and abstract lyrics although with a deeper and sometimes sensitive content. Of course, the concept is not entirely unprecedented. Fans of Aroma Di Amore and Arbeid Adelt! will immediately recognize where part of the inspiration originates. Still, Kregel succeeds in translating those influences into something that feels fresh and contemporary. “#7” sounds wonderfully Post-Punk throughout, with one of the tracks even containing a subtle nod to The Stooges. At times the music may appear somewhat simplistic, yet this is compensated by its sheer effectiveness and the dark, menacing atmosphere that runs through the entire EP. The songs gradually build toward hypnotic crescendos and repeatedly invite the listener onto the dance floor. Kregel may ultimately remain a phenomenon primarily appreciated within Flanders, but I genuinely believe the band possesses enough originality and potential to break through much further. As far as I am concerned, this is one of the finest Belgian discoveries of recent years. (Rating:8). Listen to “Dode Mus”: https://wagonmaniac.bandcamp.com/track/dode-mus
items._cn_summary: 佛兰德三人乐队Kregel的第七张数字EP延续了1980年代后朋克与新浪潮的音乐根基，歌词采用母语并融入荒诞抽象的表达方式，营造出黑暗威胁的氛围。专辑收录四首曲目，部分作品向The Stooges致敬，整体编曲简洁却富有催眠般的渐进张力。乐队将Aroma Di Amore等前辈的影响转化为现代感的暗潮声响，在同类作品中展现出较高的原创性。作为比利时佛兰德地区的独立发行，该EP契合用户对暗潮类音乐的偏好，在后朋克框架内提供了扎实的听感体验。

items.body: Tinokuknoi Arevulopapo is the new project from Lea Cummings (King Futile, Kylie Minoise, Official Music Team, etc) and Sarah Glass, who has collaborated with Lea on a few projects. The project takes its name from a character in a Philip K. Dick short story, and Irata is a single-track affair. The forty-seven-minute instrumental track shifts between droned-out moodiness, ritual alien sound-scaping, tolling ambient industrial, and beyond For the track, the pair are playing a mix of guitars, synthesisers, tenor recorder, and percussion. There is most certainly a sci-fi feel to the whole thing, and I guess references-wise think a mix of Birchville Cat Motel, My Cat Is An Alien, and early Tangerine Dream. The track shifts through several phrases, around every fifteen minutes or so. It opens with this blend of locked & malevolently tolling guitar, spacey 'n' eerily hissing synth drones, and these distant, creepy, chiming tones. We then switch into more of an alien/ethnic ritual vibe- with a mixture of twangs, darts, sweeps, and warbles. Before later shifting to blends of slow percussive clangs and angular drones. Irata is a great opening shot from Tinokuknoi Arevulopapo, and if you're looking for long-form sci-fi focused soundscaping, it is well worth a look. It would be the perfect soundtrack for reading some of Mr Dick's work or similar Sci-fi fiction
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自Irata与Tinokuknoi Arevulopapo合作的实验性器乐专辑，时长47分钟的单曲融合了drone氛围、外星仪式感音效和氛围工业元素。Lea Cummings与Sarah Glass运用吉他、合成器、中音竖笛和打击乐编织出科幻电影般的声场，结构上约每15分钟变换一次段落：从开场阴郁的空间合成器嗡鸣与诡异叮当声响，到中段外星民族仪式感的颤音与波动，再到后段缓慢打击乐铿锵声与棱角分明的合成器。参考了早期Tangerine Dream、Birchville Cat Motel等前辈风格，对Philip K. Dick短篇的文学引用增添了概念深度。这张专辑精准定位于长篇科幻氛围声音编排领域，是实验、暗黑氛围与电子音乐爱好者的理想聆听对象，尤其适合搭配阅读科幻文学作品。

items.excerpt: Ancient Future — Purple Spirits (Tributes to Musical Giants) (Ancient-Future.Com Records, 2026) On Purple Spirits, Ancient Future has gathered multifaceted and imaginative tributes to artists…
items.body:
Ancient Future — Purple Spirits (Tributes to Musical Giants) (Ancient-Future.Com Records, 2026)

On Purple Spirits, Ancient Future has gathered multifaceted and imaginative tributes to artists with historical ties to the long-running American world music fusion ensemble. The West Coast musicians present a set of cathartic pieces deeply influenced by Indian classical music, jazz, flamenco, Vietnamese traditions and rock.

The delightful “Punjabi Jhinzaki” honors tabla master Ustad Zakir Hussain, who contributed to Ancient Future’s development and appeared on the group’s album World Without Walls. Meanwhile, “Spirit Of Nirvana” addresses the group’s unexpected connection to Nirvana.

“East Of The Sun (Studio Version)” features a stellar performance by Oregon member Paul McCandless on oboe; the recording is described as his final released oboe performance after a 2017 health condition led him to retire from the instrument.

The album also includes the soulful “Tres Tarantas Tres,” a tribute to flamenco guitarist David Easley, a former Boulder High School guitar student of Ancient Future founder Matthew Montfort. 

In addition, the mesmerizing “Purple Nam” and “Purple Haze (Vietnamese Đàn Bầu Style)” pays tribute to Jimi Hendrix through Indian raga and Vietnamese music elements.

Performers include Matthew Montfort on scalloped fretboard guitar, Glissentar 11-string fretless guitar, flamenco guitar, and fretless bass; Bui Huu Nhut on Vietnamese đàn bầu; Abbos Kosimov on Uzbek percussion; Mariah Parker on keyboards and santur; Benjy Wertheimer and Aditya Kalyanpur on tabla; George Brooks on saxophone; Kai Eckhardt on fretless bass; and Paul McCandless on oboe.

Founded in 1978, Ancient Future has developed a rich catalog of world music fusion, with a rotating chamber ensemble that includes traditional musicians from multiple regions. The band’s discography includes Visions of a Peaceful Planet (1979), Natural Rhythms, Quiet Fire (Narada Lotus 1012, 1986), World Without Walls (Narada/Sona Gaia 163, 1990), Dreamchaser (Narada/Sona Gaia 154, 1998), Asian Fusion (Narada Equinox 63023, 1993), Planet Passion (Ancient-Future.Com AF 2001, 2002), Yearning for the Wind (2014).

Buy Purple Spirits.
items._cn_summary: Ancient Future成立于1978年，是美国西海岸的老牌世界音乐融合乐团。本专辑以致敬为主题，融合了印度古典、爵士、弗拉门戈、越南传统及摇滚等多种风格。专辑曲目涵盖对印度塔布拉大师乌斯塔德·扎基尔·侯赛因、涅槃乐队、弗拉门戈吉他手大卫·伊斯利及吉米·亨德里克斯的致敬，其中将 Jimi Hendrix 与印度拉格及越南传统乐器相结合的创意尤为独特。乐团成员来自多个地区，包括越南弹拨琴、乌兹别克打击乐等特色乐器演奏者。整体风格偏向世界音乐与爵士的跨界融合，具有一定的实验性和跨文化视野，符合该用户对世界音乐的偏好，但音乐表达方式相对温和，未达极端实验前沿。

items.excerpt: Warp's IDM icons resurface after 13 years with a dark, disquieting record shaped by a violent world. Say goodbye to the fuzz and wistfulness.
items.body:
Across their decades-long run as Boards of Canada, Marcus Eoin and Michael Sandison have drifted through endless shades of eerie. The Scottish brothers have been mischievous and playful, chopping up children's voices over downtempo hip-hop beats on their 1998 watershed Music Has the Right to Children and 2000's well-aged In A Beautiful Place Out In The Country. They've plunged into dark psychedelia with 2002's cryptic and sublime Geogaddi, tried melancholic pastoralism on for size in 2005 with The Campfire Headphase and teased out sinister undertones from queasy polyrhythms on 2013's lauded return to form Tomorrow's Harvest. 

With a penchant for backmasked samples and abraded synthesiser tones, the duo has historically thrived on obfuscation. This has in turn inspired a culture of eager exegesis among both fans and casual onlookers, heads tilted towards whatever they might pull off next. Their bleary, hypnotic records feel as much about what should be there as they are about what you can actually hear in the mix. 

Inferno shakes off its predecessors' shrouds, trading generalised unease for unadulterated menace. If Geogaddi continues to inspire robust discussion about its occultist allusions—it ends with a silent track to reach a runtime of precisely 66 minutes and 6 seconds—Inferno is more head-on, literally invoking demonic robot voices to read from Aleister Crowley's 1929 screed on human sacrifice. Its drumbeats and basslines slam against the ear, taking pages out of industrial and jungle's dog-eared playbooks. It's the darkest and most direct music ever issued under the Boards of Canada seal, a bold swing for an artist whose prettier early formula still inspires wan imitation to this day.

The 18-track, 70-minute LP delivers its fair share of disguised utterances, but it also draws on plenty of clear speech with disarming transparency. A few of these samples stick to familiar discursive modes: "The Word Becomes Flesh" features a documentary narrator cheerfully describing the development of an embryo, a clip that could slot neatly onto Boards of Canada's turn-of-the-millennium offerings. Others highlight speakers who seethe with dramatic conviction. In "Age of Capricorn," in the midst of a smeary choral loop, an overpowering interjection comes from an American-accented voice deep in prayer: "I'm a sinner," he declares, his words hanging plainly in the ambience. "You bore my sin. You shed your blood for me, to cleanse me."

Later, on "Father and Son," another believer speaks as if he's in the middle of a movie scene: "I love you, but I love the Lord more than any physical being," he repeats, his voice Auto-Tuned and snapped to the snaking beat. His conversation partner answers him in corroded metallic babbles reminiscent of Drukqs-era Aphex Twin. The Crowley excerpt on "All Reason Departs" opines in gravelly tones that "the great war must be fought. This bloody sacrifice is the critical point of the world-ceremony of the proclamation of Horus, the crowned and conquering child," before a dense, mechanic groove rolls through like the interlocking of several rusted gears. And on the pounding "Naraka," named after the realm of suffering in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist traditions, we hear devotees chant the Hare Krishna mantra. It's easy to forget the song bears the name of a kind of hell.
 
These are bleak expanses, to be sure. It's a heavy and at time unlovely listen, liable to jar on first contact. But there are oases to break up the wastes. "Into the Magic Land" draws upon Boards of Canada's early shoegaze influences with echoing guitar and cavernous percussion; "Deep Time," first released as April's "Tape 05," shimmers with plucked strings and wafting woodwinds. Close to the album's finish, "You Retreat in Time and Space" burbles with melodies so soft, so untroubled, that it could be drawn from lullabies. Bells twinkle. Horns blare. A beatific dawn settles over an empty plain, and terror retreats to dwindling memory. Against the turmoil of the current cultural moment, this is some of the most placid and enchanting music they've laid to tape.

As Inferno’s crests from chaos to sanctuary, the rosy picture gives way to closer "I Saw Through Platonia," an understated coda to what are otherwise largely tense and writhing proceedings. The sound that predominates in the album's final minutes is the simple recording of a human heartbeat. With this sample, Boards of Canada pinch Inferno's themes to a subtle point. Throughout the record, people speak about what they believe to be true but cannot materially observe. They make declarations about deities. They talk about Christ's return as if it were sure to happen, a forewarning with an especially dire resonance in this age of Christofascist holy war.

Here, after sharing glimpses of the world's unfolding horror intermingled with astonishing beauty, Boards of Canada drag your ear down to the sound of pulsing blood: a sound that anyone alive can hear within their own bodies. So many stories seduce, and so many are used to justify world-rending violence. What can we know to be real? The body exists. Start there.

items._cn_summary: 《Inferno》是苏格兰电子双人组Boards of Canada至今最黑暗、最直接的作品，标志着他们从早期梦幻般的氛围电子向暗潮与工业融合的转型。专辑采样了Aleister Crowley关于人祭的文字，引入恶魔般的机器人声和美式祈祷者的忏悔，配合工业鼓点与丛林节奏的撞击，构建出强烈的威胁感。18轨、70分钟的篇幅中既有隐晦的窃窃私语，也有透明如纪录片式的念白采样，延续了乐队标志性的后向采样与磨损合成器音色。这张专辑与其早期引发模仿的唯美公式形成鲜明对比，展现出激进且具有挑衅性的艺术立场，与用户的实验/暗潮/电子音乐偏好高度契合。

items.body: By Matty Bannond Google can’t introduce you to Keenan Ruffin or Stan Zenkov. ChatGPT will guess their biographical details with trademark confidence and trademark lack of accuracy. These two improvisers operate beyond the reach of data-driven detectives and AI assistants. The only way of getting to know their artistic personalities is to listen to their music. There’s rich reward for that sonic study. Ruffin is a guitarist and Zenkov plays reed instruments. Both perform frequently in Brooklyn. This four-track album, released in November 2025, captures a 45-minute session from October 2024. The protagonists pass moods and motifs around the studio, while Ruffin explores his pedals and Zenkov cycles through clarinets and saxophones. Two distinct identities emerge in sharp focus. The prevailing character of the record is affable, welcoming and generous. Ruffin often constructs arpeggio-adjacent shapes like ladders for his listeners to climb, using extended effects to add warmth rather than discord or discomfort. In the early stages of the title track, he picks notes like water droplets. Later, he stifles his strings to produce a sound like a windchime. Zenkov is more excitable and energetic but successfully avoids crowding out his colleague or overwhelming his audience. The shortest piece, “1000 Armed Massage”, has a tentative and peering-around-corners feel. It features a balladeering central section, where the bass clarinet’s plummy voice hums a melodic line as if embarrassed to have forgotten the lyrics. The third track, “Turn the Wheel”, stands out for its spookier spirit. It’s the album’s most industrialized district. Something is rotating behind the initial exchanges. Zenkov plays more hectic material, while Ruffin deploys his pedals and switches with more pugnacity. It’s a nervy, threatening piece that suggests a cornered animal with titanium teeth bared and rusty claws unsheathed. In today’s age of intrusive tech tools and aggressive data scraping, it’s impressive that Keenan Ruffin and Stan Zenkov have maintained such a low digital profile—but faintly regrettable too. These are two disarming and benevolent improvisers who share their unpretentious, open-hearted music with the world on The Mechanics of Getting Anywhere . Listeners get rich reward for time spent with this record. But don’t tell the robots. The album is available on cassette and as a digital download here . items.body: Review by The Progolyte — I had heard rumors in the community about this record being an underrated gem of the Rock Progressivo Italiano scene, so today I finally check it out. The record is called Flore Di Metallo by I Califfi, and overall I got some really nice vibes from this one. While it may not be top-tier in the world of Italian prog, it's got some really nice keyboard-based rock music with a nice twinge of excitement oozing out of it. The cover didn't seem to convey the musical identity that much, with the more moody atmosphere I got from it, but that part of this album was still pretty good as well. Moving on, I really enjoyed the musicianship and thought the personnel had a lot of talent being the classic four-man crew. It includes Sandro Cinotti on keyboards, Vincenzo Amadei on guitar, Franco Boldrini on bass, Maurizio Boldrini on drums, and then all but Sandro helps out with the vocals. The music is quite strong, having an ear-catching mix of hard rock and symphonic prog. You also get some acoustic bits on songs like Alleluia and Felicit�, Sorriso E Pianto, which seem to fit in as a counter to the much more erratic styles on other pieces. The songs do seem to be a little shorter than what I would like, but the material here is strong enough to make up for the lacking lengths. These guys sound very similar to Quella Vecchia Locanda at points, specifically the more rock-focused bits of their debut album, though they still have those classical elements floating around here and there. Tracks like Flore Finto, Flore Di Metallo, and Varius are some of the most exciting, bombastic, and interesting compositions on the album. They approach heavy jazz fusion and avant prog at points while also playing into more somber and moody tones. Other highlights on the album include the opener Nel Mio Passato and Campane, which have some really nice depth along with beginning and ending the record nicely. In conclusion, I enjoyed this one quite a bit, and I'll definitely be coming back to it more often. It's incredibly engaging with the listener and always delving deep into the musical environment of the fusions of heavy psych and wild symphonic prog, and I hope more people listen to this one soon enough. As for my final rating, I think I'll go with a mid or strong 4/5.
items._cn_summary: 意大利前卫摇滚专辑，发行于1973年，展现出键盘主导的硬摇滚与交响前卫融合风格，并融入爵士融合与先锋元素。专辑在沉稳氛围与激烈段落间交替，Acoustic段落与实验性编排形成对比，作曲家将重迷幻与交响元素自然结合。相较于主流意大利前卫摇滚，该作品更具跨界融合特质，键盘与吉他的即兴对话呼应学院派爵士的即兴精神。尽管歌曲篇幅较短，但整体音乐深度与创新性足以弥补。作为70年代意大利独立摇滚场景的代表作品，专辑在实验性与地域特色方面均有所表现，对偏好前卫与融合风格的听众具有一定吸引力。

items.body: Here, he stands swallowed by the sky Life, so small – dust in nature’s eye He seeds the ground, fallow by death’s hand Our hidden past, the fiction of all man L’Avenir has ushered in their latest album, Secrets, with the video for Animism, a coldwave séance of mineral calm and occult motion, where the air seems to have been left under overnight under a full moon, and returned with new intelligence. The Baltimore project, led by Jason Sloan, treats electronic music as architecture as much as emotion: a corridor of blue light, a stairwell descending beneath memory, a voice arriving from somewhere just beyond the visible wall. On this first single from the project’s eighth album, Sloan works with a familiar vocabulary: patient drum-machine pressure, icy synthesizers, distant singing – but the result feels newly charged, as if each element has been placed glowing under glass. Animism takes its title with admirable seriousness. The song imagines a world in which matter has memory and the inanimate keeps counsel. The earth, the tree, the old room, the object handled too often by human longing: all seem to possess a private pulse. Sloan’s voice sits inside the track rather than above it, less a guide than a presence caught in the same current as the listener. The effect is intimate and estranged, the sound of someone speaking from within a thought that has become physical. The track brings to mind the elegant austerity of Eleven Pond, the dusky romanticism of Clan of Xymox, the severe European mechanics of Parade Ground, and the cerebral chill of Trisomie 21. These references move through the song like figures glimpsed in frosted glass, recognizable but never allowed to dominate the room. The arrangement advances with a measured hand, giving each synth line and percussive motion enough space to breathe before the next cold gleam arrives. The accompanying video, directed by Soleil Noir Studios, deepens the spell. Shot by Jason Sloan, with Sloan also handling video synthesizer programming and both analogue and digital hardware, the clip turns the forests of the mind into a prismatic terrain. Bright colours bloom against mirrored images; faces and forms double, dissolve, and reassemble in a kind of psychic woodland. The imagery suggests a psychedelic passage through inner nature, where branches become nerves, light becomes thought, and perception starts to behave like a living organism. Animism presents L’Avenir as a project still devoted to solitude, mystery, and nocturnal design, but newly attentive to the strange life hidden inside surfaces. Sloan makes darkwave feel porous here, open to trees, stones, ghosts, and the quiet intelligence of everything we mistakenly believe is still. Watch the video for “Animism” below: Secrets is out now via EINS:ZWEI:ACHT on vinyl, CD, digital, and streaming formats. Listen to Animism below and order Secrets here. items.body: In the distance I am cold In the distance We’re growing old Casket Cassette’s Show Me a Sign is a song that illuminates the soul like a busted strip of Los Angeles nightlife, all neon nerves and cheap salvation. Constant Laval Williams has made a fine little art out of sounding stranded in public, which is harder than it sounds. Plenty of singers can do lonely. Fewer can do lonely while the beat is still carrying everybody’s boots across the dancefloor. This is the third new song from REDUCER, out June 12. Show Me a Sign is all reduction: emotion boiled until it stains the pan, desire shaved down to the bare request, survival turned into something blunt enough to fit in one hand. There is no grand cathedral of misery here, no velvet cape dragged theatrically through dry ice. The song wants a signal, a room, a body, a way back from whatever distance has turned the song’s protagonist cold and old before his time. Show Me a Sign channels the Medusa, Twist of Shadows, and Creatures era Clan of Xymox in its dusky romantic architecture, Cold Cave in its sleek black propulsion, and the frozen passion of The Danse Society and Pink Turns Blue, but Casket Cassette is smart enough to understand that influences should behave like a ghost at the bar, present but never picking up the tab. And the track moves with the clean, severe confidence of a dark priest descending inward into an icy sanctum, torchlit and severe, conjuring unspeakable visions as Williams’ voice cuts through the darkness. Lyrically, the song circles distance, exhaustion, and the stubborn will to continue after comfort has abandoned the room. The plea for a sign feels less like romantic longing than a last candle held against the cold, a small act of devotion made under pressure. Casket Cassette turns that ache into body music for the damaged and devout, for people who have been through Hell and back again and lived to tell the tale. Mixed by Matia Simovich at Infinite Power Studios and mastered by Stefan Brown at Abbey Road Studios, Show Me a Sign has a polished chill; every element has been placed with surgical precision: the beat advances, the synths flare and recede, and the vocal keeps its eyes open. The song’s desperation lands because it is sharpened rather than softened, with the production giving the plea force, shape, and urgency. Listen to Show Me a Sign below and order the single here. Show Me a Sign by Casket Cassette Casket Cassette will take The Reducer Tour across North America in summer 2026, with support from Stare Away and special guests. The run opens in Southern California before cutting through the Southwest and Texas, heading up the East Coast, crossing into Toronto, then moving through the Midwest, Mountain West, Pacific Northwest, and back down the West Coast, with a final date in California in November. items._cn_summary: Casket Cassette的《Show Me a Sign》属于暗潮与后朋克融合的独立音乐作品，风格上接近Clan of Xymox、Cold Cave及Pink Turns Blue等经典暗潮/冷潮乐队。乐评强调了歌曲以“reduction”（削减）为核心的美学理念，将情感提炼至极限，聚焦疏离感、疲惫感与生存意志的表达。制作方面由Matia Simovich混音、Stefan Brown在Abbey Road Studios mastering，整体声响冷冽精准。作为独立发行的暗潮作品，其与用户偏好列表中的暗潮类型高度匹配，创作上虽沿袭传统暗潮框架，但"stranded in public"的声线处理和极简主义叙事策略具有一定个人特色，整体质量扎实。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track “Springleik,” signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close.
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: Camilla Hole Trio的《Langs》在挪威民谣与爵士之间构建了一座桥梁。女高音萨克斯手Hole主导旋律线，与贝斯手Egil Kalman和鼓手Knut Kvifte Nesheim形成灵活的三重奏配置。值得注意的是，乐手角色并不固定，贝斯可演奏旋律，鼓手可拓展节奏结构。模块合成器与颤音琴的叠加为传统民间素材增添了现代色彩，使"Springleik"这样的西挪威舞曲呈现出即兴化的演绎方式。从前作《Eventyrferd》的科幻探索转向更接地气的表达，但实验精神仍在角色轮换与即兴段落的交错中延续。这种民谣、爵士与电子元素的跨领域融合，对于关注前卫爵士和世界音乐融合的听众而言具有吸引力。

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we’d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow— both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That’s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched.
items.reviewer: Recordings and Commentary by Ian Brennan
items._cn_summary: 这张由伊恩·布伦南制作的作品超越了传统音乐范畴，是一份来自芝加哥枪支暴力幸存者的街头录音文档。二十五位直接受暴力影响的社区居民参与录制，包含即兴说唱与真实声响的混合。作为声音艺术与社会文献的跨界作品，其实验性体现在对现实素材的直接使用，而非传统音乐结构的构建。这种极致的非传统形式契合实验/前卫的审美取向，但作为非音乐性内容在评估上有所限制。作品以社区参与为核心，呈现了艺术介入社会议题的可能性。

items.excerpt: Polish artist Maria Ka’s latest album Di Mashin (The Machine) emerged after she found that her family had Jewish roots – a discovery that led her to an immersion in Jewish studies and the Yiddish language. She unreels original songs written in Yiddish, embracing a politically active feminism and a committed meta-universality. Her musical vision is fragrantly mystical and musically all encompassing.

items._cn_summary: 波兰艺术家Maria Ka在发现家族犹太血统后，深入研究犹太文化与意第绪语，以此创作专辑《Di Mashin》。作品用意第绪语呈现原创歌曲，融入政治性女权主义视角，音乐风格兼具神秘主义气质与包罗万象的实验性。作为融合世界音乐与当代实验的作品，其跨文化视角和语言独特性具有一定价值。RootsWorld的评论对音乐描述较为有限，但从有限的文本可看出该专辑兼具传统意第绪语音乐根基与创新性表达。

items.excerpt: The Visit isn’t an album built on compromises. Composer-musician Cris Derksen, a Canadian from the North TallCree Reserve on her father’s side, and with a Mennonite lineage from her mother, pushes and cajoles her visions. She’s primarily a cellist, one who works across genres – one of the great joys of listening to The Visit is that it is impossible to attach any kind of handle to the music. Just as you think you have it nailed down, the next track is something different.

items.excerpt: Richard Wileman (Karda Estra) has joined forces with English folk singer Chantelle Smith for a new folk horror album titled Samhain Tree. The duo has…
items.body:
Richard Wileman (Karda Estra) has joined forces with English folk singer Chantelle Smith for a new folk horror album titled Samhain Tree. The duo has unveiled the first single, “Wheel Of Fortune,” alongside a mesmrizing video featuring scenes filmed around Avebury in southwestern England.

Smith and Wileman previously collaborated on Wileman’s 2024 solo album The Forked Road. After those sessions, the pair decided to continue working together and develop a new collection of unconventional folk songs and instrumentals. Their material draws from experimental ambient improvisation, traditional storytelling, and darker folk influences.
items._cn_summary: Richard Wileman与Chantelle Smith合作的《Samhain Tree》专辑首支单曲《Wheel Of Fortune》展现了一种融合实验氛围即兴与传统民间叙事的音乐路径。作品取材自英国西南部的Avebury地区，结合黑暗民间元素与叙事性歌词，呈现出介于实验与民俗之间的独特气质。这种将实验性音响与传统故事性结合的做法，与用户偏好的实验、前卫及暗潮风格存在一定交集。尽管音乐内容在融合度上具有一定吸引力，但评论信息较为简略，未能深入展开音乐细节与创作背景，仅停留在新专辑发布的新闻层面。

items._cn_summary: 《Alive Alone, Alive Together》是布鲁克林实验吉他手Ava Mendoza的新作，八首曲目中有七首为之前专辑的重编版本，其中2021年器乐专辑《New Spells》与2024年《The Circular Train》中的曲目经重新编排后获得新生。专辑邀请到自由爵士名将Hamid Drake担纲鼓手，将噪音摇滚、自由爵士与实验即兴元素相融合。Mendoza在过去二十年间通过Unnatural Ways、Bill Orcutt Guitar Quartet及个人创作积累了深厚的实验声誉，此次重编企划展现了旧作在新语境下的声音可能性与即兴碰撞的张力。作为独立厂牌发行、来自非主流音乐圈的音乐人，其跨类型融合的实验性符合目标用户的前卫与爵士口味，唯重编版本占比高而新鲜素材有限。
