items.body: Review by TenYearsAfter — Ruud Dielen had a long history with cover bands , playing guitar in songs from Jimi Hendrix, Santana, Led Zeppelin, Queen, Toto and Genesis. After many years touring in the more commercial circuit, he decided that it was time to write his own music and in 2017 he produced his first album entitled Aquarius, as a one-man-band (guitar, bass and synthesizers), under the name Glorious Wolf. The music sounds as a tribute to the Seventies era progrock and Classic Rock, from Pink Floyd to Zappa and Hendrix, embellished with a wonderful array of vintage sounds (from Moog, Mellotron and Hammond to Gibson, Fender and Mesa Boogie). On his second album Zodiac (2019) and third Mysterious Traveller (2023) Ruud started to invite male and female singers, and to blend the progrock sound with a more song-oriented and varied musical attitude. On Prog Archives Ruud Dielen his Glorious Wolf project got a lot of praise for that musical formula, meandering tastefully and elaborately between instrumental Old School vintage keyboard drenched progrock and song-oriented tracks. And now, anno 2026, here's Ruud again (playing acoustic - and electric guitars, fretless bass, Precision bass, synthesizers, mellotron and FX drums) with Glorious Wolf, featuring a range of national and international guest musicians, on vocals, drums, bass, Hammond, Yamaha piano, Mellotron, theremin and saxophone. Most of the foreign musicians Ruud had met during an international musical collaboration.Elements of Hope Pt.1 ? Instrumental (4.34) : This new album starts with an exciting electronic music atmosphere featuring pulsating sequencers and spacey synthesizers, then howling and biting Gilmourian guitar runs, topped with Mellotron choirs, followed by a tight and catchy beat. The music is embellished with Ruud his powerful guitar runs, fat synthesizer flights and soaring Mellotron choirs, and backed by a fluent rhythm-section (Kike Paglia on drums and Tim Ros on bass). In the end majectic Mellotron choirs erupt, wow, what an impressive start!Elements of Hope Pt.2 - Carrying this Yoke (6.15) : The intro delivers psychedelic sounding Mellotron violins. The music turns into a folky climate with acoustic guitar and fragile English male vocals (by Frank van der Borg), in a slow rhythm. Gradually a more lush sound featuring Mellotron violins, and powerful vocals and guitar riffs. In the final part a break with raw guitar riffs and propulsive drum beats. Lots of contrast, variety and dynamics, and tastefully arranged.Elements of Hope Pt.3 - Into the Clouds (5.55) : First celestial female vocals (by Jyoti Verhoeff) and twanging acoustic guitar, in a dreamy and hypnotizing climate, wonderful. Now the sound becomes more lush, embellished with fretless bass, slow drumbeats and distinctive female vocals. Gradually the atmosphere is working to a symptuous climax with a synthesizer solo, powerful drums and Hammond, culminating into fiery guitar solo, how exciting.Elements of Hope Pt.4 ? Instrumental (1.42) : A short piece in an ominous climate, with raw and powerful guitar, and slow and powerful drumbeats, the interplay is awesome.Elements of Hope Pt.5 - Life's Chaotic Spell (5.51) : The final part of this 5-pieve epic title track contains omnipresent Hammond, blended with exciting rock guitar, powerful male English vocals and a propulsive rhythm-section. Now saxophone play (by Reg Parham) joins, strongly coloring the music, with hints from Frank Zappa and King Crimson. Finally a heavy guitar solo, backed by a dynamic rhythm-section and Hammond.If You Please ? instrumental (6.20) : This composition delivers a slow rhythm and a compelling climate, Ruud really shines with his guitarwork, from sensitive to fiery, and using the tremolo-arm and wah-wah pedal, prog meets bluesrock, wow. Halfway beeps and bleeps, then a more atmospheric sound featuring spectacular wah-wah driven guitar runs, backed by propulsive drumbeats.If I Only (5.46) : After an intro with Mellotron (by the late Thomas Zunk) and militairy drums the music turns into a slow rhythm with heavy guitar, strong male vocals and gradually a more bombastic atmosphere. Halfway a fiery guitar solo, with howling and biting leads and Hammond layers, the music builds and builds, very compelling and exciting.Whirlwinds & Maelstroms ? instrumental (6.44) : Another Mellotron soaken intro, then slow drumbeats and powerful guitar. Halfway a swirling Hammond solo (XK5 Hammond with Leslie by Harry Knapen), followed by a heavy guitar solo, the interplay is excellent.Everything Must Break to Grow - EoH Pt.2 Reprise (6.25) : The final track on this new album starts with dreamy piano and vocals, then a slow rhythm, in a melancholical atmosphere, topped with subtle slide guitar. Gradually the sound turns into more lush and powerful featuring rock guitar and a dynamic rhythm-section. Finally dreamy with spacey synthesizers, guitar and voices, another example of Ruud his interesting and varied musical ideas.In the 3 years after his previous effort Ruud has moved and built a high-tec studio in his new home. You can hear the result: a mature and elaborate new album on which the music is wonderfully meandering between Old School prog and a more varied and song-oriented musical approach, embellished with his awesome guitarwork, vintage keyboards and vocal leads, and backed by good musicians. After Edo Spanninga (as E.D.O.) with his solo album The Past Is A Foreign Country, his other project Trion with Terra Tiempo here is another excellent new Dutch prog effort, well done Ruud!
items._cn_summary: 《Elements of Hope》延续了Glorious Wolf项目对七十年代前卫摇滚的致敬，融合了平克·弗洛伊德式的迷幻氛围与弗兰克·扎帕式的实验精神。整张专辑以复古模拟合成器（Moog、Mellotron）为骨架，配合现代电子音乐常用的音序器和空间音效，营造出复古与当代交织的声响景观。三个篇章各具特色：开场以纯器乐展现电子氛围与吉普尔式吉他速弹的碰撞；中段转入民谣化的原声吉他与细腻人声，形成动态对比；末段则以前卫摇滚的华丽编曲达到高潮，融入萨克斯、泰勒明琴等特色音色。从口味匹配度来看，该作品精准契合用户的实验/前卫偏好，跨越了经典摇滚与电子音乐、渐进摇滚与世界音乐（荷兰与多国音乐家合作）的边界，具有较高的创新融合价值与艺术完成度。

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — According to ProgArchives, Il Bacio Della Medusa's sophomore album, Discesa Agl'inferi D'un Giovane Amante, is the not only the greatest Rock Progressivo Italiano record of the 21st century, but also one of the greatest progressive rock albums of the 2000s overall (as of writing this, it stands in the top 50 albums between 2000 and 2025). I had incredibly high expectations going into this, because I honestly thought modern rock progressivo italiano couldn't get better than Logos and Unreal City, so I was indeed hoping for a masterpiece. And somehow, it could get better than those. This is hands down the absolute pinnacle of modern Rock Progressivo Italiano and one of the finest pieces in the subgenre. It holds beauty, tragedy, insanity, and power all tied into an imaginative and epic journey. The music found on here is very sophisticated and well crafted, with there being an overwhelming sense of classical influences scattered across the record as the band also pays tribute to the classic Italian bands of the seventies, all with a new twist of horror and stunning visuals the music can put into your mind when listening to it. The entire album consists of 12 individual tracks, but they all function as one continuous composition. The first two tracks, Preludio: Il Trapasso and Confessione D'un Amante, actually have no drums and are more akin to mellow and sometimes even romantic-sounding chamber music, and they do an amazing job at introducing the listener to what music here will sound like and acting as the calm before the storm. From here on out, most of the remaining tracks are just absolutely astounding, and each has a staggering amount of details with incredibly intricate arrangements spliced into every moment. The titles of these pieces are each quite lengthy and depict very vivid pictures about the concept of this record, but in the end the long titles don't bother me when the music here is this good. Numbers like La Bestia Ed Il Delirio, Ricordi Del Supplizio, Nostalgia Pentimento E Rabbia, Sudorazione A Freddo Sotto Il Chiaro Di Luna, and so many other tracks are legitimately some of the strongest Rock Progressivo Italiano I've ever heard, and it's phenomenal the way the band never misses a beat when it comes to keeping the energy and atmosphere going for each one. Each of these and the other ones have everything I could've ever wanted from an Italian album. Raspy vocals, vibrant flutes, intense, unhinged heavy-rocking electric guitars, and even soft and sweet acoustic and classical guitars combined with passionate string work. I really enjoyed how the band balances all the deranged and unpredictable parts with the charmingly quiet yet moody ones. The music is always developing and never stops growing and pushing into different sectors of the story, and it always changes the mood perfectly with the musical direction, and the mind-blowing talent of how these musicians play their instruments throughout the whole is also just the cherry on top for the whole thing. In conclusion, I completely agree with ProgArchives in that this album is truly a remarkable piece of art. Maybe not a completely perfect masterpiece, but definitely a near-perfect masterpiece! Going into this, I knew the album was supposed to be good, but I honestly didn't know it would be THAT good. This is in between a high 4.5/5 and a low 4.75/5 and is a must-listen for any fans of progressive rock, not just of Italian progressive rock. And one more note, this is surprisingly the only Italian album to achieve my "Number 1 album of the year" award, that year being 2008.
items._cn_summary: 这张意大利进步摇滚专辑融合了古典音乐元素与70年代经典意大利摇滚传统，属于前卫摇滚范畴。专辑以12首曲目构建连续叙事，前半部分采用无鼓的室内乐形式，后半部分转向复杂编曲的摇滚语言，涵盖粗粝人声、长笛、电吉他和弦乐等元素。其音乐构思带有恐怖与视觉意象，编曲细腻且不断演变。对于偏好实验与前卫音乐的用户而言，该专辑提供了一定的探索空间，同时保留了意大利进步摇滚的地区特色与概念专辑的叙事结构。

items.body: Dass von einigen Musikern gilt, dass sie stets mit neuen Ansätzen überraschen, mag selbst so eine Phrase sein. Bei Will Yates alias Memotone stimmt das in dem Punkt, dass er seinen Ansatz tatsächlich von Platte zu Platte verändert oder zumindest verschiebt. Ob das dann noch für Überraschungen taugt oder schon zur erwartbaren Konstante gerät? Was auf Warm Shadows ganz sicher unerwartet kommt, ist der Fortgang von Stück zu Stück. So lässt die Titelnummer am Anfang vermuten, dass Yates seine Klarinette erneut in verschiedenen Zusammenhängen erkundet, mit sich langsam vorantastendem Jazz und einer elektronischen Verfremdung des Blasinstruments, die an eine Verneigung in Richtung Jon Hassell denken lässt. Gleich im nächsten Song, ja, doch, singt dann die litauische Musikerin Ugnė Uma nach einem gesprochenen Monolog über verhaltenen einzelnen Gitarrentönen und einem ostinat im Hintergrund tackernden Rhythmus, der weniger Beat als durch diskretes Zittern tragende Zeitstruktur sein möchte. Der Beat versteckt sich auch in der folgenden Nummer, die man als Improvisieren mit Ambient-Elementen deuten kann, ohne dass klar ist, was für Instrumente da genau zum Einsatz kommen – Streicher? Echte? Konstant bleibt auf der Platte die friedliche Grundstimmung, die zugleich von unaufhörlicher Neugier getrieben scheint. Da kann man zwischendurch schon mal bei einer Indie-Rock-Nummer landen, die derart aufs Knappste arrangiert ist, dass sich beim besten Willen keine Rock-Klischees darin finden. Überraschung. Gute.
items._cn_summary: 英国制作人Memotone（Will Yates）的专辑《Warm Shadows》延续了其不断探索新路径的创作理念，将单簧管的爵士即兴与电子声响巧妙融合，并邀请立陶宛音乐家Ugnė Uma贡献人声与spoken word段落。专辑在曲目间呈现显著的风格跳跃——从氛围电子到极简indie-rock，从即兴演奏到ambient节奏结构，整体保持平和内省的气质同时又充满不竭的好奇心。作为欧洲独立厂牌发行作品，其声音设计精致且具实验性，跨界融合了爵士、电子、世界音乐与当代作曲元素，与用户的实验、前卫、爵士及电子口味高度匹配。尽管部分段落可能稍显零散，但其不落俗套的编曲策略避开了常见的风格窠臼，展现出独特的艺术自觉性。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — While the heavy hitters of Spanish prog in the 1970s nosedived directly into the crafty fusionpossibilities of the Rock Andaluz scene which commingled the disparate worlds of flamenco andprogressive rock, the Basque region of Spain and France was a different story altogether. The Basqueculture (and language) is one of the few isolates in all of Europe predating the arrival of allthings Indo-European and therefore has remained steadfastly independent in its own world which hasproven to cause a lot of friction in recent decades but as far as the music scene was concerned, theacts that emerged from the 1970s prog scene in the northeastern corner of Spain were more than happyto adopt outsider influences however instead of looking to the flamenco fusion of Andalucia, thecrafty jazz fusion and symphonic prog acts of Madrid and Barcelona or even the Celtic influences ofCantabria, the majority of the Basque groups utilized the region's own folk traditions to mix andmingle with the sounds and flavors of progressive rock.While the bands Itoiz, Haizea and Errobi are the best known out this scene, the more obscureMAGDALENA that emerged from the bull running city of Pamplona-Iru�a and named after the neighborhoodwhere it rehearsed created its own unique distinct style that not only merged the disparate worldsof Basque folk music and progressive rock but unlike its contemporaries openly invited theAndalusian flamenco sounds into its mix albeit in a subdued manner. This band was active from 1978 -81 and managed to release its sole album LANEAN SARTZEN which ironically means "Getting Started" inthe exact year that the band ceased to exist. The band was unusual in that it featured threeguitarists that included Jos� Arcaya, Jos� Luis Pastor and Javier Ib��ez along with bassist CarlosGalindo, drummer Nando Abadia "Ringo" and Mikel Landa who played both the flute and clarinet. Whileprimarily dedicated to complex instrumental motifs that incorporated jazz, prog and folk, vocalsperformed in the Basque language did appear courtesy of the two guitarist Iba�ez and Arcaya.Sounding really unlike anything else from the Spanish prog scene or anywhere else for that matter,MAGDALENA was quite unique in that it featured melodic triple-guitar harmonies reminiscent somewhatof the technique of Wishbone Ash however steeped in prog and Basque folk musical complexities. Theslight symphonic touches with flamenco undertones and aspects of jazz allowed a fairly uniquetapestry of stylistic effects and with the inclusion of light airy flutes and clarinet, the bandexuded a rather eclectic style that while similar to bands like Enbor, Lisker, Errobi or Sakre,MAGDALENA offered a more complex style of progressive folk rock that complimented the region's moreindependently minded acts. While the album is more on the folky flutey side of things, more rockoriented songs do exist with the track "Rokanrol" appearing as the rowdiest rocker on board althoughthis particular track is also the least complex and the more straight forward rock song on board.MAGDALENA was the most famous of the local Pamplona scene and revered in certain circles for itsinnovative eclectic blend of ethnic folk music infused with prog and jazz. On LANEAN SARTZEN theband demonstrated a high level of maturity in not only the exquisitely designed compositionalfortitude but also in the excellent instrumental interplay that allowed the band to engage in bothmelodic harmony-based musical motifs as well as making hairpin turns into more off kilter proggymusical cadences that set this band well apart from the more traditionally minded folk rock bandsthat existed in the area at the time. When all is said and done the band managed to keep its localfolk traditions in tact on this sole release while infusing its music with wild and daringprogressive elements. For my personal tastes this band suits me the most out of the Basque prog rockand folk acts that i've come across so far. While compared to the lighthearted approach of theBarcelona symphonic act G�tic, in reality this band was as much as a musical isolate as the cultureit emerged from.
items._cn_summary: 这张发行于1981年的专辑展现了西班牙巴斯克地区独特的前卫民谣风格，将当地传统音乐与渐进摇滚巧妙融合。乐队采用三吉他编制，呈现类似Wishbone Ash的三重旋律和声技法，同时融入爵士元素和弗拉门戈的低调色彩，辅以长笛和单簧管编织出清新而复杂的声音纹理。巴斯克语歌词演唱为专辑增添了鲜明的地域文化特征。整体风格虽与Enbor、Errobi等同期巴斯克乐队有相似之处，但三重吉他配置和融合了安达卢西亚元素的独特尝试使其更具实验性和辨识度。对于偏好世界音乐与前卫融合的听众而言，这是一张具有独特文化价值的地下遗珠。

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — Continuing to parallel the career path of the related HEXVESSEL but, unlike that group, feistily clinging to its acoustic derivations, this solo project of Finn Jesse Heikkinen has almost convinced me to learn some music editing software so I can splice and dice to accentuate the wurst and suppress the worst. This is overall an appealing amalgam of Nordic hard rock verging on metal and ponderously strummed acoustic reveries, but not always juxtaposed artfully. The surprise appearance of Seattle based neo folker KING DUDE in "Forgiveness Undone" is more than just an exploit of name recognition, as the warmth of his baritone is just what such an angry piece craves. "The Forsaken Oath" might be on similar lyrical streams but is elevated later by weighty synth work, and "Mona Lisa Smile", as much as its title predisposes me to shun it, is actually an accomplished piano ballad made all the more effective for its scarcity in the ITERUM NATA repertoire. "Heartwood is Dead" is another repeat button number, as much because I can't place where I have heard a near identical melody as for its inherent merits. The closer rehashes a trune from the debut album, luckily a good one.Beyond this, "Mooncry Symphony" and "I Have been Sacrificed" alternate the shadows and hazy light with mixed success, with some astounding CAMEL-like bluesy guitar and vocal interludes reminiscent of the German DICE meets MOODY BLUES, but failing the consistency test, notwithstanding the A for effort.A superior exercise along similar lines to 2024's "From the Infinite Light" and sidling up to 3.5 stars, "Heartwood", while possessing the necessary BPM, is a bit too arrhythmic to receive my wholehearted endorsement, but maybe that's the point.
items._cn_summary: 这是芬兰音乐人Jesse Heikkinen的个人计划延续，延续了与HEXVESSEL相关的职业路径，但更坚守原声音乐根源。专辑融合了北欧硬摇滚、前卫金属与沉思式原声音景，在不同时代音乐元素间游走。评论者指出部分曲目如"Mona Lisa Smile"的钢琴ballad段落展现了艺术性，而"Mooncry Symphony"和"I Have been Sacrificed"则呈现CAMEL式的蓝调吉他与声乐穿插，混合了德国DICE与MOODY BLUES的韵味。作为2024年"From the Infinite Light"的延续作品，这张专辑在实验性与可听性间取得了一定平衡，虽未达到完全一致的质量，但展现了北欧前卫民谣的独特魅力，适合对世界音乐与实验融合感兴趣且能接受金属元素的听众。

items.body: Review by kev rowland — Once this has been played it is easy to understand why it is rated on ProgArchives as one of the top albums from 2025 as it captures the proghead from the beginning and refuses to let go. Master composer and keyboard player/vocalist Anthony Kalugin has again used a host of guests to bring his concept to life, and utilising the vocal talents of Richard Sinclair on two songs is a masterstroke as he still sounds just like he did on 'Breathless' nearly 50 years ago. But he is not the only 'name' involved, as Michel St-P�re (Mystery) is one of the guitarists, John Hackett is on flute, and other singers include Jean Pageau (Mystery), Bartosz Kossowicz (Collage, Quidam), Marco Gl�hmann (Sylvan) and Olha Rostovska who has been involved with Karfagen for years.The result is a highly polished symphonic prog album with neo, and crossover influences divided into two parts of virtually equal length with six songs in the first and four in the second. There is a lightness throughout with no feeling of ego or self-contemplation. It is a prog album which is actually very easy to listen to, although never easy listening. The use of multiple singers does mean it has somewhat of a project feel to it, but musically all involved work closely together without any feeling of disconnect and while I cannot imagine many of the musicians actually worked in the same studio at the same time, it never comes across in that manner. There is some truly wonderful orchestration at times, with "Mirror of Souls" (which ends the first part) coming across as Camel crossed with classical and is simply beautiful.Kalugin has a very high output with multiple projects, but his quality is just as high as his quantity, and this is a modern progressive album with deep roots which is a joy to hear.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自乌克兰音乐家安东尼·卡卢金的概念专辑，融合了交响前卫摇滚与新古典 crossover 风格，邀请了理查德·辛克莱尔、约翰·哈基特等多位知名音乐人参与。专辑采用双部分结构，共十首曲目，强调精致编排与流畅聆听体验。亮点在于「Mirror of Souls」等曲目中将 Camel 乐队气质与古典元素相融合，营造出优美的管弦乐氛围。整体制作精良、层次丰富，但实验性较为保守，更偏向传统交响前卫路线。对于偏好实验与前卫风格的用户而言，该专辑提供了扎实的技巧展现与舒适的听感，适合作为现代交响前卫的标准参考作品。

items._cn_summary: Loop Finding Jazz Records是德国实验音乐家Jan JelineK以爵士唱片为素材进行循环采样与重构的概念专辑，属于实验电子与学院派爵士的跨界融合。艺术家通过解构既有爵士录音，创造出碎片化、循环往复的声响结构，展现了高度的概念性与实验性。尽管Boomkat标注了来源，但正文内容缺失，无法获得更详实的评论信息。该作品定位偏向小众实验听众群，契合用户对实验/前卫音乐及学院派爵士的口味偏好，整体风格独特且具有创新价值。

items.body:
Hearing Jason Kruk for the first time on Len Davis’s Bitches Brew was a jolt - the kind of discovery that sends you searching for more. His new album, Beyond the Veil is a bold, highenergy fusion statement featuring an allstar cast with guitarists Adam Rogers, Wayne Krantz, and Snarky Puppy Alumni Michael League, Bob Lanzetti.




The album wastes no time reeling you in. Rogers ignites “Awakening” and “The Lion” with sharp, commanding guitar lines, while “The Ox” leans into a deep funk pocket before exploding into a standout electricpiano solo from Hirahara. Krantz brings his signature edge to “The Eagle,” delivering a thrilling mix of singlenote runs and angular chord work. “The Man” channels the spontaneity of a live jam, while “Dad” offers a moment of calm with atmospheric textures and understated rhythm work. “Water” is one of the album’s highlights - a constantly evolving piece that moves from a gentle intro to intense, tightly woven interplay. “Wind” and “Fire” keep the heat on with virtuosic soloing and a rhythm section firing on all cylinders.
The closer, “Creation,” takes its time to find direction, but once it locks in, the band delivers a powerful final stretch that rewards listeners who stay with it.




Throughout, Kruk’s drumming is the engine: precise, muscular, and always pushing the music forward. Beyond the Veil is memorable, energetic, and packed with standout performances - a musthear for fusion fans and one of 2026’s early high points.




Favorite Tracks: “The Eagle,” “Wind”

 LIKE 4
Louis Stewart: Joyce Notes
By Ian Patterson
May 23, 2026
View read count
Few books have provoked such acclaim and disdain as Ulysses (1922), James Joyce's dense and dazzling opus.

Banned in the UK, subject to an obscenity trial in the USA, scrutinized, vilified and glorified, it has inspired and baffled in equal measure. Its experimental stream-of-consciousness style—liberally laced with puns and mordant humor—has proven a literary Everest for many, an indigestible slog for others. Even Joyce's wife allegedly observed: "Why don't you write books people can read?"

With its rattling, coiling rhythms, vivid soundscapes, lyricism and deeply observed humanity, Ulysses is also a work ripe for musical interpretation. Luciano Berio and Anthony Burgess both took the plunge. Likewise, Irish jazz musician Ronan Guilfoyle's large-scale work "Counterpoints"—premiered in 2013 —was inspired by the musicality in Joyce's prose. And then there is guitarist Louis Stewart's Joyce Notes.

Dubliner Stewart (1944-2016) was best known as an interpreter of standards—a jazz guitarist with few peers. Jim Hall and Martin Taylor were both admirers. And, thanks to Livia Records' reissues of Stewart's long-out-of-print discography, a host of modern six-stringers such as Mary Halvorson, Kurt Rosenwinkel, Ant Law and Eleonora Strino have also fallen under Stewart's spell. Equally known for his wit, it is easy to see how Stewart would have gravitated towards Joyce, though his Joyce Notes extended work—funded by an Irish Arts Council Award to mark the writer's centenary in 1982—marked a departure from his customary musical habitat.

Recorded live at the Cork Jazz Festival in 1982, Stewart leads an eight-piece jazz ensemble through an hour-long suite inspired by various episodes from Ulysses. Stewart's old sparring partners Jim Doherty (piano) and Peter Ainscough (percussion) are joined by Americans Steve LaSpina (bass) and veteran Bobby Rosengarden (drums) in a swinging rhythm section. Up front, Richie Buckley (tenor saxophone), Len McCarthy (alto saxophone) and Brian Dunning (flute) revel in the spoils of improvisation. This was Stewart's only completely self-composed project in his career, and he seems content, in the main, to stoke the rhythmic fires. When he does solo, notably on "Stephen" and "Molly"—where Rosengarden's fills conjure cartwheels rattling over cobblestones—he lifts the ensemble around him.

Central to the success of the suite is narrator Eamon Morrisey, whose clipped Dublin tones relay scenes from Joyce's book. It is no easy task to translate the myriad rhythms of the characters' speech, emotions and subconscious voices; drunken sailors, capricious students, world-weary prostitutes, dreamers and hopeless romantics come and go against the sonic backdrop of bustling, cosmopolitan early-20th-century Dublin. Morrisey pulls it off quite brilliantly, catching the current of humor that runs through Ulysses like one long seam of gold.

Special mention too for flautist Dunning, whose melodious virtuosity is another constant delight. Anyone intrigued by Dunning could do worse than lend an ear to the reissue of the Louis Stewart-Brian Dunning collaboration Alone Together (Livia Records, 2025), where the flautist arguably outshines his more illustrious senior.

Joyce Notes remains a one-off in Stewart's discography, but it is more than a mere curio. Its charms may well entice waverers to dive, fully committed, into Ulysses' depths, while making a compelling case for Stewart as a composer and conceptualist who hid those particular talents under a bushel.

items.body: We are asking the questions, we are lying to get by We are lying on our backs, wondering about the sky We are blind when it suits us, we still hear the noise Are these delusions of our making? Is this the illusion of choice? Every life eventually arrives at the same locked door: the one behind which the meaning of it all is supposed to be waiting. As the years burn, we gather love, pleasure, machines, money, memories, and little mementos of our existence, only to find the old questions still standing there, untouched, and unanswered. With “All We’ve Known of Heaven,” Soft Vein turns that existential ache into a sleek new wave confession, one lit by bright synths, bruised romance, and the uneasy knowledge that abundance does not always equal salvation. The second single from his forthcoming new album continues Justin Chamberlain’s recent evolution into a more refined, sophisticated synthpop silhouette. Where earlier Soft Vein material often leaned heavily into darkwave gloom, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” moves with a more cinematic sense of yearning: a sighing, almost church-like introduction opening into a pulsing bass synth, rippling electronics, and a breathy vocal performance that feels suspended between confession. The song follows the previously released single Chekov in placing Chamberlain’s voice and writing at the center. The production, co-produced by Chamberlain with Andrea Mantione of Nuovo Testamento, has the sheen of expensive glass and the anxiety of someone staring straight through it. There is an unmistakable 1980s charge here: a nocturnal, Michael Mann-like glow; the elegant propulsion of new wave pop; and vocal harmonies that call to mind the grand emotional sweep of Simple Minds without slipping into too much of their new gold sheen. Lyrically, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” circles the elegant catastrophes of modern life: desire, consumption, spiritual exhaustion, the little betrayals people commit simply to keep moving. The song asks what remains when everything has been acquired except meaning. Its central question — “Is this all we are?” — becomes less a cry of defeat than a flare sent into the cogs of our disconnected digital existence, in search of a sign of life beyond our modern appetites and illusions. That tension gives the track its strange pull. Soft Vein writes about a world in which modern convenience has multiplied beyond imagination — machines for pleasure, endless means of contact, every appetite fed on command — yet we seem no closer to one another, and no nearer to knowing anything like heaven. The song understands excess as both seduction and trap: the comfort that dulls us, the desire that divides us, the little betrayals people commit while searching for warmth in the wrong rooms. By the time Rachel Mazer’s saxophone arrives near the finale, it feels like a final flare of feeling inside all that machinery: romantic, wounded, and gone almost as soon as it appears. Mastered by Jason Corbett of ACTORS, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” suggests a Soft Vein expanding in real time, stepping further into an 80s pop architecture while keeping a darkwave pulse beating beneath the floorboards. There is a compelling parallel in Producer Phil Thornalley’s own arc, from the Gothic depths of The Cure’s Pornography era to the gleaming new wave heights of Johnny Hates Jazz. For Soft Vein, that kind of range does not feel like a contradiction or retreat, but the natural continuum of any good artist: a movement from severity to sophistication, from dread to desire, from the basement to the bright lights without losing the ache underneath. Listen to “All We’ve Known of Heaven” below: All We’ve Known of Heaven by SOFT VEIN Follow SOFT VEIN: Website Instagram Facebook Bandcamp Spotify The post “Is This All We Are?” — Soft Vein Shares Existential New Wave Single “All We’ve Known of Heaven” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: Soft Vein 是以 Justin Chamberlain 为核心的个人项目，这首单曲融合了 synthpop 的制作质感与新浪潮的复古美学，带有暗潮音乐的阴沉氛围和电子合成器的主导声响。歌曲探讨现代生活中的存在主义困境，在消费主义与灵性疲惫之间寻找平衡。制作团队与独立暗潮圈子（ACTORS、Nuovo Testamento）有一定关联，音乐中可见 1980 年代新浪潮的典型特征如电子音色和合成器流行结构。虽有复古情怀与哲学深度，但在创新性和实验性方面表现有限，属于暗潮与电子音乐交叉领域的常规作品。

items.body: Króta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Edén has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sjøfløyte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects.

items._cn_summary: 专辑《Króta》由一位瑞典提琴手和两位挪威音乐家合作，演绎两国传统民间曲目。音乐家们均具有跨界背景，包括挪威先驱乐队Slinkombas的早期实验经验。演奏中融入了萨克斯风、风笛等非传统乐器，展现出将北欧民谣与当代音乐语境融合的尝试。尽管本质仍是传统曲目改编，但在演奏方式上呈现出一定的开放性。发行于挪威独立厂牌Taragot，符合小众厂牌特质。对于偏好实验与创新的听众而言，该专辑提供了传统民间音乐与多元风格的交汇点。

items.excerpt: This collaboration between the five-piece Belgian instrumental group Wör, whose members specialize in bringing the music of earlier centuries to life, and Kongero, the acclaimed Swedish female a capella folk quartet, offers an unusual chance to explore how their two cultures, ostensibly so different, can come together. items._cn_summary: 比利时历史音乐组合WÖr与瑞典女声阿卡贝拉民谣四重奏Kongero的合作现场专辑，探索欧洲不同文化背景下的音乐对话。WÖr致力于呈现早期几个世纪的音乐风貌，Kongero则专注瑞典传统民谣的阿卡贝拉演绎，两者在RootsWorld评论中被描述为“音乐上的最佳朋友”。虽然这是一次跨文化的融合尝试，契合用户对世界音乐的兴趣，但作品本质仍是传统/历史音乐与传统民谣的合作，实验性与创新性相对有限。比利时与瑞典均为欧洲音乐发达地区，无法获得地区特色加分。评论内容较短但提供了有意义的文化比较视角，适合对欧洲传统音乐跨文化融合感兴趣的听众。

items.album: Beck, Mexican Institute of Sound and Meridian Brothers Join on “Ritmo Babilonia”
items.excerpt: Mexican Institute of Sound and Meridian Brothers have released “Ritmo Babilonia,” the final single from their collaborative album Ruido Tovar. The track features Beck and…
items.body:
Mexican Institute of Sound and Meridian Brothers have released “Ritmo Babilonia,” the final single from their collaborative album Ruido Tovar. The track features Beck and reimagines Rigo Tovar’s 1981 song “El Festival De Mi Pueblo.”

Rooted in late-1970s and early-1980s Mexican tropical music, Ruido Tovar examines the period when artists began replacing traditional instrumentation with synthesizers. Camilo Lara and Meridian Brothers leader Eblis Álvarez completed the album during a weeklong session at Lara’s studio in January 2025.

“Ritmo Babilonia” is one of two Beck collaborations on the album. The recording bring together percussion and keyboards from Pachi Sánchez and Lauro López — members of Costa Azul, Tovar’s original backing band — with Beck’s vocals and Lara’s production.

Beck said his connection with cumbia stretches back to childhood experiences in East Los Angeles. “Camilo played me Meridian Brothers years ago, and I loved it,” he said. “A lot of my childhood was around East LA. Cumbia has been in the background my whole life.”
items._cn_summary: Mexican Institute of Sound与Meridian Brothers合作的《Ritmo Babilonia》探索了1970至1980年代墨西哥热带音乐向合成器时代的转型期。专辑重新诠释Rigo Tovar 1981年的作品，邀请Beck参与演唱，体现了跨艺术家的融合创作。该作品符合用户对世界音乐与电子融合的兴趣，合成器与热带节奏的结合具有实验性。然而评论内容较短，信息量有限，仅涉及单一单曲而非整张专辑，且为新闻稿性质，难以全面评估创新深度。地区特色加分适用（墨西哥拉丁美洲背景），但评论质量修正拉低了一定分数。

items.body: Im Jahr 1969 wurden »die kulturellen Barrieren, die Japans zahlreiche Künstler:innen und Entertainer:innen lange voneinander getrennt hatten, endlich beseitigt«, schrieb Julian Cope 2007 in seinem bisweilen zweifelhaften, aber doch essenziellen Japrocksampler. Das Jahr sei ein Wendepunkt gewesen und habe ein neues Zeitalter der Experimente eingeläutet, dessen Ergebnisse »unglaublich energiegeladene Werke hervorbrachten, von denen sich viele jeder Kategorisierung entzogen«. Far East New Rock Invention 1969–1975, veröffentlicht als Teil der Wamono-Reihe von 180g, dokumentiert die Genese dieser neuen Sounds. Unter den neun Stücken finden sich bekanntere Vertreter wie die Far East Family Band, Yuya Uchida & The Flowers und deren Nachfolger, die Flower Travellin’ Band – hier in Kollaboration mit dem Terumasa Hino Quintett –, größtenteils stammen sie aus dem Katalog von Nippon Columbia. Viele der zugehörigen Alben wurden zuletzt neu aufgelegt. Die Zusammenstellung zielt offensichtlich darauf ab, diese lose Bewegung, die ihre Inspiration aus Hard- und Psych-Rock, Folk und gelegentlich der Avantgarde-Musik bezog, einem breiteren Publikum nahezubringen. Doch auch die Heads können darunter Nuggets entdecken, beispielsweise Cuts des The-Dynamites-Mitglieds Hiroshi Segawa sowie Takeshi Inomata & Sound L.T.D.s rasender Jazz-Fusion-Freak-Out »Black Angel«. Far East New Rock Invention ist die Art von Compilation, die ihr Publikum dazu animieren will, tiefer zu diggen. Das lohnt sich ja.
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑汇集了1969至1975年间日本摇滚发展的重要曲目，涵盖Hard Rock、Psych Rock、Folk以及偶发的Avant-garde元素。收录了Far East Family Band、Yuya Uchida & The Flowers、Flower Travellin' Band等代表性艺术家作品，其中部分与Jazz Fusion跨界融合，如Takeshi Inomata & Sound L.T.D.的《Black Angel》展现了爵士与摇滚的交织。专辑以历史文献视角呈现日本摇滚在吸收西方音乐后的本土化探索，兼具娱乐性与研究价值。虽以摇滚为主体，但Avant-garde实验性有限，与用户偏好的实验/前卫、学院派爵士存在一定距离。对于关注世界音乐融合及日本摇滚历史的听众而言具有参考意义。

items.body: Although primarily known as a Bach interpreter, pianist Simone Dinnerstein and her string ensemble, Baroklyn, find a natural affinity for the music of Philip Glass, the subject of Hourglass, her first recording for the Naïve label. Yet affinity alone hardly explains the uncanny sense of inevitability that permeates these performances. What emerges instead is a meeting of imaginations preoccupied with the strange elasticity of passing moments and the hidden variations between them. In the album booklet, the ensemble’s leader observes that every repetition in Glass reacts to what preceded it while anticipating what follows. Nothing remains static. “We hear it as a constant becoming,” she writes, “not as a set of musical facts.” That idea becomes the philosophical axis of the recording. More than a play on the composer’s surname, Hourglass evokes matter suspended within time’s narrowing chamber, each grain brushing against countless others on its descent. Dinnerstein approaches Glass not as a minimalist sculptor of patterns but as a composer of tides and gradual transformation. Her playing reveals an art founded on metamorphosis. The Suite from “The Hours” (2002) opens the album in a state of exquisite unease. The source material already carries the weight of fractured interior lives, yet what emerges here reaches beyond narrative into something almost cosmological. Upper and lower strings move in subtle dislocations, circling one another like celestial bodies uncertain whether they approach union or catastrophe. Beneath them, the cellos sway with a dignified grief. At the center of this emotional system burns no triumphant sun. Instead, one encounters the afterimage of a dying star, its radiance stretched thin across immeasurable distance. The musicians understand the necessity of restraint, receding whenever needed so that Dinnerstein’s piano may gather the evaporating particles left behind by the strings before they disappear into the surrounding dark. Every phrase feels suspended between touch and extinction. What astonishes most is the music’s sense of disembodiment. It hovers just beyond ordinary consciousness, brushing against intuitions the intellect cannot fully stabilize. Glass is often reduced to discussions of process and structure, yet these performances uncover something deeply organic beneath the repetitions. Each figure develops its own ecology, its own gravitational field. Dinnerstein shapes the motifs as living terrains whose contours shift under changing light. Time transforms recurrence into an altered emotional space. Every return carries traces of what came before. Meanings accumulate gradually, through accretion rather than declaration, until each phrase seems to open inward toward another hidden chamber. A passage of fluttering trills briefly alters the atmosphere. Suddenly, there are birds suspended over immense fields, flashes of earthly tenderness interrupting the work’s abstraction. Yet even these remain touched by remoteness. The violins continue drawing the listener deeper into an immense interior cosmos where emotion belongs to matter itself. Part II emerges from the husk of those earlier sorrows with newfound translucence. The strings unfold in slow waves, allowing the piano to float upon their surface as both reflection and witness. A faint harmonic shift changes the coloration of the entire landscape. The transition into Part III possesses the delicate instability of waking from a dream whose images resist immediate translation. The piano searches through ascending gestures that feel at once anxious and ceremonial. Dinnerstein renders these moments with extraordinary sensitivity to weight and spacing. She never hurries revelation, allowing uncertainty to linger long enough to become attractive. And then, the melodies release us as gently as they first gathered us. One leaves the suite with the sensation of having crossed through several seasons in a single night. The recording quality deserves particular praise. The keyboard exists both within the orchestra’s collective body and apart from it, intimate yet unreachable, a consciousness wandering among other consciousnesses. Harp and celesta enter with spectral luminosity, altering the chemistry of light itself. From there, we enter the denser terrain of the Tirol Concerto for Piano and Orchestra (2000). Ostensibly Glass’s first piano concerto, the work balances inheritance and subversion, acknowledging a grand tradition while quietly hollowing out many of its assumptions. From the opening’s shifting, sand-like textures, the listener is drawn into a landscape haunted by premonitions of Glass’s later Étude No. 13. The immense second movement forms the emotional core not only of the concerto but of the album itself. Spanning nearly 17 minutes, it unfolds with the patient majesty of something unconcerned with ordinary temporal measures. There is nothing exhibitionistic about its beauty. Few scores in Glass’s output achieve this degree of aching translucence, and the present recording approaches it with reverence unmarred by sentimentality. Midway through the movement, ascending scales rise with almost unbearable clarity. Their motion suggests release while remaining tethered to gravity. Dinnerstein articulates these passages with crystalline poise, allowing every note to refract like sunlight entering deep water. As the mood recedes into dissonance, the landscape changes once again. And by the time the final movement arrives with its dancing contours and coiling energies, joy has become inseparable from experience. Earlier shadows remain present within every gesture of exuberance. Yet Glass refuses the simplicity of triumph. Even heroism rests on the back of fragility. Such maturity gives the concerto its enduring power: resolution emerges not through conquest but through recognition that every forward motion leaves something behind. Throughout Hourglass, Dinnerstein reveals herself not merely as an interpreter of Glass but as someone capable of exposing an underlying metaphysics. Too often, discussions of his music become trapped within debates over minimalism, repetition, accessibility, or influence. This recording bypasses those exhausted categories entirely. It restores mystery to music that many listeners assume they already understand. The natural reaction to all this is not simply admiration for the performances, extraordinary as they are, but a heightened awareness of time’s strange interiority. Glass and Dinnerstein seem less interested in measuring duration than in revealing how the human soul inhabits it. The hourglass does not merely count passing grains. It transforms motion into memory. Perhaps that is why this music lingers with such unsettling force. It reminds us that identity itself may consist of endlessly repeated patterns altered by the invisible pressures surrounding us. We return to familiar thoughts, believing them to be unchanged, only to discover they now contain the dreams of another life. Hourglass is set for release on June 5. items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the key players in the Ona Laietana (Laietan Wave) of Catalonian jazz fusion, ORQUESTRAMIRASOL was one of the earliest acts to emerge in the world of jazz fusion getting its start in 1973before the collapse of the Franco regime a couple years later. This group was amongst manyfusionists emerging from the Barcelona region with this band coming out of the nearby city of SantCugat del Vall�s with the band name resulting from a neighborhood in that city. The band releasedtwo well regarded albums in its short two year existence before morphing into a more Latin musicinfused offshoot called Mirasol-Colores. This debut SALSA CATALANA appeared on the Zeleste label andwas primarily inspired by the American fusion scene mining influences from the likes of Chic Coreaand Return To Forever as well as The Weather Report and Herbie Hancock. One of the more melodic and groovy of the Barcelona fusionists, ORQUESTRA MIRASOL eschewed the overtcomplex excesses of some of the most demanding European fusion acts and aimed to deliver moretraditional jazz structures intertwined into the context of progressive rock with both the lightairy aspects of The Weather Report in connection with the jazz funk styles of Herbie Hancock but asfar as the piano work goes the primary source of inspiration is clearly Chic Corea. In addition tothe foreign imports on board, this band eschewed the temptation of jumping n the Rock Andaluzbandwagon and instead looked towards the folk inspired sounds of the Mediterranean thus delivering asomewhat unique example of Spanish jazz fusion.The album is on the light and airier side of the equation. While not exactly commercial in nature inthe vein of Herbie Hancock's "Headhunter" with catchy funk grooves and ear wormy hooks, the band didblend its complexities in a fairly seamless manner which allowed an organic flow of ideas unlike thejitteriness of bands yet to come such as M�sica Urbana and others. The album features seven tracksand is quite short at only 33 minutes of playing time. The lineup included Xavier Batl�s (bass),Victor Ammann (piano), Ricard Roda (sax/flute/synthesizers), Pedrito Diaz (percussion), and MiquelLizandra (drums). The album makes full use of flute sounds offering some folk lightheadedness whilethe percussion delivers both the typical rock style of drumming as well as lots of Latin musicalcomponents and while not salsa as the album title might connote, the album does sound like the styleis intricately woven into the mix.Another aspect that this band was known for was that some of the keyboard parts were reminiscent ofEngland's Canterbury scene and at key moments refer to the works of 70s era Soft Machine but thebass grooves typically remain funk fueled but do venture off into a more hard bop stylistic approachas well. Notably absent are the sounds of guitars which exemplify the cleaner sound that the bandstrived for and although the bass and drums anchor it into the world of prog rock, the album's lackof heavy distortion makes it sound ethereal much like the band G�tic would deliver on its debutrelease down the road. It's an eclectic yet accessible style of fusion performed by this fascinatingband that despite its brevity delivered an exhilarating dose of high quality fusion that harkens toits references across the pond yet finding its own distinct methodology of blending it all together.One of the Spanish fusion acts that sounded more rooted in jazz than the rock elements. This is ahighly enjoyable debut.

 LIKE 2
Bobby Broom: Notes Of Thanks
By Jack Bowers
May 25, 2026
View read count
Guitarist Bobby Broom is no stranger to the music of tenor saxophonist Sonny Rollins, having spent two tours of duty with various Rollins groups which, taken together, add up to a decade (1982-'87 and 2005-'10). Notes of Thanks is Broom's way of expressing his gratitude to Rollins for those years in the trenches and the many valuable lessons he learned there, the best way he knows how: through his music.

Rollins wrote every song on Notes of Thanks save one, bassist Dennis Carroll's easygoing "Me Time." The third member of Broom's Chicago-based trio is drummer Kobie Watkins. Even though Broom is among the best at what he does, and his teammates are likewise sharp and skillful, there is only so much a trio can do to engender variety, no matter how perceptive and charming the music.

With that in mind, it should be noted that there are not many guitar-led trios as proficient as this one, and that Rollins' tunes are for the most part astute and engaging, starting with the good-natured "Alfie's Theme" (not to be confused with the "Alfie" written by Burt Bacharach and Hal David for the 1966 film of that name), on which Broom delivers the first of his sharp and measured solos, enhanced by a brief nod to Joshua and the battle of Jericho.

"The Freedom Suite, Part 1" is next, followed by one of Rollins' more well-known tunes, the amiable and rhythmic "Doxy." Carroll takes one of his admirable solos there, while Watkins displays his deftness at the drum kit. It is not until later—the last two numbers, in fact—that Broom and his mates delve into any other Rollins classics, namely the high-stepping "Pent Up House" and canorous "Valse Hot." They are preceded by the lesser-known "Allison," "Kim," "Paul's Pal" and "Strode Road."

A largely agreeable studio session for trio (and Rollins) fans with an extra half-star for exemplary teamwork and musicianship.

Alfie's Theme; The Freedom Suite (part 1); Doxy; Allison; Kim; Me Time; Paul's Pal; Strode Road; Pent Up House; Valse Hot.

Home » Jazz Articles » Album Review » Sue Cahill: Evanstonia

 LIKE 4
Sue Cahill: Evanstonia
By Mike Jurkovic
May 23, 2026
View read count
Double bassist/composer Sue Cahill's Evanstonia kicks off with one of those olde-tyme a-ratta-tat-tat and a-ratta-tat-tat courtesy of drummer Dru Heller (Don Byron, Greg Osby) that can sweep a listener off into one of those musical moments that lock in at the moment, escort attention elsewhere for a while, then return one safely to the moody environs and everyday routine.

Evanstonia is a mellow bit of magic. It is never truly meant to challenge, but it is hardly derivative and hardly without surprise and vast delight. "Violet Snow" evolves into a thoroughly engaging journey through the aging process to vintage. And it all takes place after the chamber-esque discordance that opens the track.

As explained in the press material, Cahill sets aside her university teaching and orchestral underpinnings on Evanstonia to flourish in the fertile flatlands of theory and improvisation. So an ominous tango like the lustrous "Serenata" sounds right at home against the poppy ruse of "Unpresidented," and the sweeping romance of "Blue Light."

Of Evanstonia 's seven Cahill compositions, it is perhaps "Fading Into Autumn" where the composer and her music owes a hefty debt to the deft trio the bassist has assembled to support her. Pianist Dawn Clement (Matt Wilson, Buster Williams) is so much of one voice with Cahill that one might, in fact, first think the bassist's main instrument was the piano. It is lush. It is romantic. It is responsive and reactive. It is Cahill's second voice. Meanwhile, the drummer unfolds both shadows and the light, popping here, shuffling there, ready at any moment to take the lead or release it.

Though "June-February" may be meant as the emotional peak of the 'personal music' Cahill pursues on the album, it is, unfortunately, the most distracting track. Sung by pianist Clement, the lyrics are those of loss and resiliency." The tune moves solemnly, beautifully, meaningfully. But it breaks the enduring spell of the album's six previous gems.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自希腊克里特岛的Stelios Petrakis，他被视为当地传统乐器——克里特 lyra 的顶尖演奏家。专辑以抒情为主题，展现了该地区传统音乐的丰富旋律与音色层次，邀请了同等水准的音乐家参与伴奏。对于偏好世界音乐与民间融合的听众而言，这是一张扎实的传统世界音乐作品，强调文化传承与技艺展示。不过，从创新性与实验性角度来看，专辑更偏向遵循传统框架，在跨领域融合与声音实验方面着墨有限，缺乏前卫或跨界的大胆尝试。

items.album: Hear65's guide to concerts and gigs to catch in Singapore in 2026
items.excerpt: Looking for a gig where you can let loose after a long week at work? Or do you require a fresh idea for a weekend date with that special someone in your life? With a variety of live music events already added to the 2026 calendar, you can rest assured that you will find something that suits your needs. If you are not sure where to start looking, here is a guide to concerts, gigs, festivals, and events featuring homegrown musicians and artists that you can catch on our sunny island this year. UPC
items.body: Looking for a gig where you can let loose after a long week at work? Or do you require a fresh idea for a weekend date with that special someone in your life? With a variety of live music events already added to the 2026 calendar, you can rest assured that you will find something that suits your needs. If you are not sure where to start looking, here is a guide to concerts, gigs, festivals, and events featuring homegrown musicians and artists that you can catch on our sunny island this year. UPCOMING GIGS Candlelight Concerts When : Various dates Where: Various venues Tickets: More information is available here Fever 's celebrated Candlelight Concerts series is back in 2025 and music lovers can expect to be mesmerised by classical renditions of tunes from beloved films, hits from some of the biggest names from the international music scene, and more. This year is all about tributes to legendary music soundtracks in movies and dramas by the likes of Hans Zimmer , Coldplay, Ed Sheeran & more. RUPTURE When : 28-30 May 2026, 6:30AM Where: Empress Lawn Tickets: Free entry The Observatory are set to usher in the break of dawn with a rare free performance at the Singapore International Festival of Arts 2026 . Titled RUPTURE , the immersive work draws from volcanic activity, seismic research, and mythology, transforming field recordings from volcanic sites and seismic data into shifting sonic textures that mirror cycles of destruction and renewal. Framed around the myth of Prometheus — “the thief of fire, the first disruptor” — the performance unfolds as night gives way to morning, with sound structures rising and collapsing in real time. Conceived as a ritualistic daybreak experience alongside three suns & moons, the set sees the band exploring “geological and emotional” seismic shifts through a liminal space where perception feels heightened and unstable. Lush Life When : 29-30 May 2026, 8PM Where: Victoria Theatre Tickets: $48 - $88, available here Two of Singapore's most iconic and contrasting voices share one stage in a groundbreaking new work. Helmed by internationally acclaimed Singapore director Ong Keng Sen known for his distinct aesthetic in creating documentary performance through collaboration with his performers and extensive research, Lush Life is an intimate documentary piece that weaves the lives, artistry and connections between the sublime, audiophile-grade jazz of songbird Jacintha and the bohemian spirit of pop icon Dick Lee . Through personal narratives, archival traces and live music, this distilled work paints a dual portrait of artistic and life pursuits. Sink into the lush world of Jacintha's music and Lee's vibrant classics, revealed as chapters in their lives. Lush Life is a conversation across styles and generations, a meditation on what it means to live a creative life in its most resonant form. Earthopia Fest 2026 When : 29-31 May 2026, 10AM Where: Fort Canning Green Tickets: Free entry, register here Earthopia Fest 2026 is set to return, bringing together a vibrant mix of live music, sustainability, art, and community action. Headlined by acts including Shye , Club Mild , Sobs , Heema Izzati , and Jukuleles , the three-day festival will also feature thrift and circular fashion pop-ups, eco-focused workshops, interactive art installations, yoga sessions, and insight talks by youth-led organisations and sustainability advocates. Curated as a space “that turns apathy into action”, Earthopia Fest promises an immersive weekend where festival-goers can discover new music, support conscious brands, and connect with Singapore’s growing creative and environmental communities. Identité When : 29 May 2026, 7:30PM Where: RASA Tickets: $30 Long-running independent gig series Identité continues its new chapter at RASA with another stacked night of noise, grit, and underground energy. After several well-received shows at the club over the past few months, the collective returns with aanother spectacular lineup featuring post-shoegazers SEER , groove / metalcore outfit KITASUKA , punk rock vets Iman’s League , and ska legends Cesspit . That Incredible Gig In May When : 30 May 2026, 6PM Where: Wire Entertainment Live House Tickets: $19.90, available here Organisers Wicked Productions have put together an incredible gig in May simply called... That Incredible Gig In May ! The stacked lineup includes local faves suc as rathmock , Tariot , MAO.A , Saving Medusa , Cakar and Mantra . Housekeeping When : 30 May 2026, 7PM Where: Filmhouse Tickets: Free entry After a month of filling Singapore’s newly opened arthouse cinema Filmhouse with music, movement, and late-night energy, the venue is closing out its opening run with one final blowout: Housekeeping night. Expect fuzz, groove, distortion, and rhythm to take over the space as a stacked lineup of homegrown acts — Fickle , Tomo Blu , Krunkle , Bellied Star , and ABSRD. — bring the live heat, alongside DJ sets from Disco Hue , failtrylagi , and New Masculine . Entry is free, with pay-as-you-wish donations welcomed for one last loud, sweaty, and emotional night on the floor. goneMUNE: AVERDONIA [EXTENDED] LIVE When : 30 May 2026, 10PM Where: Empress Lawn Tickets: Free entry goneMUNE brings the metal heart of AVERDONIA to life with goneMUNE: AVERDONIA [EXTENDED] LIVE , a fleshed-out continuation of the darkwave world first introduced in their self-titled album. The performance will feature new tracks alongside music from AVERDONIA , with Mervin Wong joining the live set and Tactility of Light handling lights. The gig is part of SIFA x Big Duck Music , alongside performances by Hidemen and Houg . Fans can also dive deeper into the origins of AVERDONIA through an accompanying exhibition by AxTL x HOTHOUSE (running from 7-15 May ), which explores the project’s beginnings through surround sound and immersive lights, alongside works by Alina Ling , NONFORM , Hidemen , and Houg . hello risk hello reward When : 6-7 June 2026, 8:30PM Where: Esplanade Concourse Tickets: Free entry He greets risk with a hello, but is unsure of his reward. The first step is always the scariest. Doubts run freely in his head, untamed. His judgement of foresight is veiled by irrational fears. Despite this, he maintains a cool composure on the outside. He forcibly silences the noise in his head, while diving headfirst into the aforementioned risk. Join deførmed as he performs his first ever soliloquy, of which the narrative is guided by his songs. BIG BIG small small When : 6-7 June 2026, 2PM, 4PM, 7PM, 9PM Where: Studio Theatre, School of the Arts Singapore Tickets: $48 - $56, available here Blending sound, sculpture, and storytelling, BIG BIG small small is an immersive, genre-defying performance that brings together Joanna Dong , Chok Kerong , and Dawn Ng in a striking exploration of existence and identity. Designed as a fluid experience rather than a conventional show, the piece invites audiences to move through a darkened, sculptural soundscape where music, spoken word, and visual art intersect — dissolving the boundaries between concert, installation, and ritual. Through bilingual compositions and a constantly shifting environment, the performance reflects on the paradox of being both small within the vast cosmos and expansive within oneself, offering an intimate yet thought-provoking journey that lingers long after the final note. Ma mère l’Oye: SNYO with Singapore Ballet When : 12-13 June 2026, 7:30PM Where: Esplanade Concert Hall Tickets: $20 - $50, available here Following their well-received 2023 collaboration, the Singapore National Youth Orchestra (SNYO) and Singapore Ballet reunite for Ma mère l’Oye: SNYO with Singapore Ballet . They jointly present the ballet piece titled Ravel Vignettes , choreographed by three of Singapore Ballet’s dancers and performed to Ravel’s enchanting Mother Goose and Schubert’s Second Symphony , the latter choreographed by the legendary Choo-San Goh . Music Director Joshua Tan also conducts the SNYO for the concert opener, Brahms’s Academic Festival Overture . A Pale Decrepit Dot Live When : 27 June 2026, 7:30PM Where: Esplanade Annexe Studio Tickets: $40 - $45, available here Amateur Takes Control confronts the fragility of existence head-on with In A Pale Decrepit Dot , their acclaimed 2025 album that laments the currency of the human condition amid a world consumed by violence, chaos, negligence, and suffering. This upcoming show will see the band deliver an immersive 80-minute set featuring material from their latest album alongside compositions from earlier releases, promising an emotionally charged journey through their evolving sound. Joining them for the night are fellow KittyWu acts I Am David Sparkle and genre-defying artist deførmed . Singapore International Piano Festival 2026 When : 2-5 July 2026, various times Where: Victoria Concert Hall & Play Den, The Arts House at The Old Parliament Tickets: $28 - $88, available here Presented by the Singapore Symphony Orchestra (SSO) , the Singapore International Piano Festival (SIPF) returns for its 32nd edition under new Artistic Director Albert Tiu . With the theme “The Pianist, Composer and Improviser”, the festival spotlights artists who perform across all three roles through six recitals, a masterclass, and two talks. Highlights include new late-night recitals at Play Den , where Singaporean pianists Churen Li (2 July, 10PM) and Jonathan Shin (3 July, 10PM) take the stage. Li’s Echoes and Refractions blends her own compositions with works by Mozart, Beethoven and Saint-Saëns, while Shin’s Restless Natures features world premieres by himself and Nathaniel Parks alongside music by Andres, Boulanger and Muhly. Broadway Beng 20th Anniversary TWENTY POON PIPI When : 10-11 July 2026, 7:30PM Where: Esplanade Concert Hall Tickets: $88 - $198, available here Blow your whistle - as the wonderful worlds of the Broadway Top Hat and the Ah Beng Gold Chain come together for the 20th anniversary celebration of our beloved Broadway Beng ! This July, elevated by a mini-combo orchestra, this East meets West, Hokkien spewing, Broadway crooning, YAN TAO (gorgeous) local superstar takes to (drumroll pls ....) the Esplanade Concert Hall ! With his hallmark tongue in cheek humour and his feet tapping, heart stopping, honey-dripping vocals, YOU die die cannot miss this Full Tux, Full Luxe affair! You must catch tok kong mini orchestra, sibeh chio Chio Buuuuuus plus the one and only Sebastian Tan as your Broadway Beng ! items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — HAIZEA (means "wind" in Basque) is one of the more recognized names when it comes to Spain's late70s progressive folk scene from the Basque region and existed from its formation in Hondarribia in1975 until its demise in 1980. The band released two distinct but vastly different albums duringthat time with this self-titled debut more in sync with the Basque folk revival scene that dominatedthe 1960s while the band's second release "Hontz Gaua" explored more daring experimental excursionsinto the world of electric psychedelic folk with much more complex arrangements. While the bandexperienced quite a few lineup changes during its five year run, amazingly the band's two albumsfeatured mostly the same members including vocalist Amaia Zubiria, guitarist / vocalist Xabier Lasa,bassist Gabriel Barrena and drummer Carlos Busto. This debut would be the only album for guitarist /vocalist Txomin Artola who would be replaced with flautist / guitarist Xabier Iriondo on the band'ssecond album.Prog lovers will probably find little interest in this debut as the band was still very much in thetraditional folk revival stage of the previous decade however with all the Basque musical flavorscorrupted by the experimental commingling of progressive rock and psychedelia imported from abroad,this debut does give a crisp clear glimpse into what the world of unaltered Basque folk actuallysounds like and that would be very similar to a lot of other European folk structures despite theBasque language and culture emerging as an anomaly isolate on a continent long overtaken by Indo-European tribes conquering the Paleolithic cultures. Obvious references on this lead to British folkacts such as The Pentangle or Steeleye Span however Basque folk sounds more similar to Celticflavors from not only Spain but the Breton region of France and of course Ireland, Wales and partsof Scotland. No bagpipes here though!While the second album was a crash course in how to update your traditions in the brave new world,HAIZEA's debut is the polar opposite of keeping things as authentic as possible with gentle folkrock instrumentation, a timeless atmospheric presence with all the tracks heavily rooted in the mosttraditional Basque folk melodies sounding much more like a Smithsonian Folkways release ofhistorical recordings than a so-called modern day progressive band but nonetheless the band performsbeautifully with a light airy feel that finds dual male and female vocals trading off along withgentle acoustic arrangements. While the the instrumentation is almost exclusively acoustic, snippetsof electric guitar do seep in on tracks like "Ura Ixurirk." The most notable different betweenBasque folk music and other European flavors is the strange rhythmic patterns that emerge from theband singing exclusively in Euskera, the native term for the Basque language.While this will not be considered essential for those seeking the more adventurous undertakings ofthe second release, this album is beautifully performed and for lovers of ethnic folk musicalexpressions i can't think of a better place to dive into the little known sounds of Basque folklorethan this debut by HAIZEA. The band's name which means "wind" really does shine though on this debutas the album passes by like a nice gentle breeze near the northern coast where Spain and Francemeet. Although there are few traces of anything progressive or experimental on this one it still isworth exploring simply as a point of reference as to how the Basque folk style was incorporated intothe context of prog rock and psychedelic folk from not only the band's sophomore release but themajority of other bands that were jumping on the progressive bandwagon after the collapse of theFranco dictatorship. The final track "Arrosa Xuriaren Azpian" at ten minutes with psychedelicovertones provides a vital clue to the band's next step. As an ethnic music lover i find this onequite pleasant as music like this is like a time machine that gives a glimpse into the collectivesoul of a culture even though i much prefer the good juicy experimental stuff!
items._cn_summary: HAIZEA是1970年代巴斯克地区传统民谣复兴运动的代表乐队，这张1977年同名专辑以原声音乐为主导，采用巴斯克语演唱，男女声交替呈现传统民谣旋律，整体风格更接近1960年代的民间复兴运动。与英国民谣乐队The Pentangle、Steeleye Span有相似之处，但巴斯克语的独特节奏模式和古老文化背景赋予其欧洲边缘地带的异域色彩。专辑中偶有电吉他点缀，但整体编制轻盈朴素，更像是一部音乐人类学文献而非前卫实验作品。对于偏好实验与创新的听众而言吸引力有限，但其作为巴斯克传统音乐的珍贵记录，在世界音乐范畴内具有一定文化研究价值。

items.body: Belgian duo Gare Noir is driven by Sam Claeys and Frits Standaert, both also known for their involvement with Red Zebra. After Red Zebra pressed the pause button, the pair began working on their own material, which first resulted in a series of singles and eventually culminated in the release of their debut album “This Is Gare Noir”, featuring twelve tracks. It quickly becomes clear that both musicians draw heavily from the golden era of the 1980s and the New-Wave movement, yet they manage to inject enough personality and individuality to make the album feel remarkably diverse. Starting from a foundation of New-Wave and Post-Punk, the duo occasionally takes detours into Pop and Rock territory, creating a record that constantly shifts in mood and texture. The entire album is masterfully stitched together, alternating between harder moments and more ethereal passages. Several songs evolve toward genuine climaxes, largely thanks to strong arrangements, clever build-ups, and the sheer power of certain choruses. The charismatic vocals naturally add even more strength and identity to the material. Above all, however, these songs radiate a sense of enjoyment and spontaneity. At times, I can hear traces of Ultravox blended with elements reminiscent of Heaven 17, before the album gradually moves into darker and more distinctive territory. Personally, I would not have minded if the album had leaned even further into darker atmospheres, but it is clear that “This Is Gare Noir” aims for a broader audience rather than confining itself to a specific niche scene. (Rating:8). Listen to “We Spin”: https://wagonmaniac.bandcamp.com/track/we-spin
items._cn_summary: 比利时二人组合Gare Noir的首张专辑融合了1980年代New Wave与Post-Punk根基，偶有流行与摇滚风格的跨界尝试。专辑展现出精心编排的结构、层次分明的情绪递进与有力的合唱段落，演奏与演唱均具备一定辨识度。乐评指出其作品兼具多样性与自发性，风格上可追溯至Ultravox与Heaven 17等经典。然而从用户偏好的实验/爵士/电子/世界/暗潮等维度审视，该专辑虽有Post-Punk基底与暗色气息，但整体更偏向复古怀旧而非实验性突破，融合跨度有限，与追求前卫创新、跨领域混搭的听众期待存在一定距离。

items.body:
Aasmund Nordstoga og Åsmund Reistad – Tom Duley og andre viser (Lydpressa, 2023)

Aasmund Nordstoga (born 1964) and Åsmund Reistad (born 1969) are a Norwegian duo with a 25-year performance history. Their collaboration began in the folk music trio Trispann and continued through Reistad’s guitar work on multiple Nordstoga solo releases. Together, they have toured widely in Norway, appearing at festivals, cultural centers, conferences, and local events, with a repertoire suited to both large stages and intimate venues.

Their duo debut, Tom Duley og andre viser, draws its material from Hartvig Kiran’s 1962 Norwegian songbook of the same title, a collection of North American folk songs translated into Norwegian. The songs gained particular traction among Norwegian singer-songwriters in the 1970s and have been less frequently performed in later decades.

On the album, Nordstoga and Reistad present warm individualized interpretations crafted during their long-running partnership. The core format is vocals and guitar, expanded by Reistad’s additional instrumentation, including bass, percussion, piano, and accordion.

Musicians: Aasmund Nordstoga on vocals; Åsmund Reistad: vocals, all instruments, arrangements, production.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由挪威民谣二人组Aasmund Nordstoga和Åsmund Reistad演绎，收录了Hartvig Kiran 1962年编选的北美民歌挪威语译本。这些歌曲在1970年代的挪威歌手圈中曾广泛传唱，专辑意在复兴这一传统。音乐采用人声与吉他为核心，辅以贝斯、打击乐、钢琴和手风琴等配器，呈现出温暖而个性化的诠释。整体制作工整、风格传统，但缺乏实验性或跨界融合元素。对于偏好实验、爵士、电子或暗潮的用户而言，这部作品更接近纯粹的北欧传统民谣改编，在用户口味匹配度上属于中等偏下。

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Silverthorn' is the tenth studio album from Kamelot as well as their first one with then-new leadsinger Tommy Karevik, previously of Seventh Wonder. This is a conceptual record, as many other worksfrom the Tampa, Florida-based symphonic power metal band, and the story revolves around the death ofa little girl and her twin brothers' witnessing this accident, based sometime in the XIX century.Stylistically, this powerful release continues an exploration of more sophisticated, almostprogressive-oriented arrangements, as heard on albums like 'Ghost Opera' and 'Poetry for thePoisoned'. Of course, Kamelot's recognizable symphonic power metal is on full display on'Silverthorn', but this album genuinely impresses with the overly technical guitar playing, the darkbut brisk atmosphere (which is at times quite cinematic, too) and the really subtle goth-rockundertones.Tommy Karevik sings excellently and as other listeners have observed, is a great fit for the band,despite the obvious similarities between him and former frontman Roy Khan. Longtime Kamelot fanscould assess more justly whether or not this is a good thing, but the songwriting and the productionon 'Silverthorn' seem to be a bit flat compared to previous albums of theirs, making this onesomewhat tedious and samey, especially in the middle. Nevertheless, the album starts off nicely,with powerful songs like 'Sacrimony' and 'Ashes to Ashes' establishing an epic and adventurous soundthat is later taken up and expanded on 'Veritas', on the title track, and on the excellent closingepic 'Prodigal Son', a gorgeous progressive experiment indeed. All in all, this is one of thesereally good but not so characteristic modern metal albums that bombast you with powerful riffs andupbeat melodies but rarely impress you as groundbreaking. I believe that Kamelot fans wouldappreciate this record the most.
items._cn_summary: Kamelot乐队第十张专辑《Silverthorn》延续其标志性的交响力量金属风格，同时融入更为精致的技术性编曲与前卫元素，呈现出暗黑但轻快的氛围及微妙的后朋克暗潮底色。新主唱Tommy Karevik的加入带来良好表现。专辑作为概念专辑，围绕十九世纪小女孩意外死亡的悲剧故事展开。然而，乐评指出其歌曲创作与制作相比前作略显平淡，中间段落存在单调感，整体缺乏突破性创新，对于口味偏向实验前卫、爵士电子与暗潮融合的听众而言，该专辑属于主流力量金属范畴内的合格之作，但创新性与跨界融合程度有限。

items.body: Having enjoyed Gimeno’s recent recordings of Bartók (Toronto SO/Harmonia Mundi – review) and Messiaen (Toronto SO/Harmonia Mundi – review), I was keen to hear this new album with the Luxembourg Philharmonic, where Gimeno served as Music Director from 2015–2025. This same artistic team released an all-Dutilleux album in 2024 that included Tout un monde lointain played by Jean-Guihen Queyras. That work, like the concerto on this new release, was written for and premiered by Mstislav Rostropovich. Lutosławski / Bloch Amazon Presto Apple Concerto for Orchestra is the best-known work from Lutosławski‘s early period: the harmonic language is dissonant but tonal, with melodic writing that reflects his study of Polish folksong and the use of older Baroque and Classical forms. The bass drum thwack that opens the Intrada has tremendous impact, signaling a wide and deep soundstage. The layered contrapuntal string entries that follow show Gimeno’s care for textural transparency, though I wanted more snarl from the brass interjections. Indeed, throughout the concerto there were moments where I craved a more garish response from the brass, though the orchestra’s gossamer colors around 5’12” are sensually impressive. The scurrying Capriccio highlights the unanimity of the orchestra’s playing, and Gimeno is sensitive to the darker, mysterious notturno e arioso passages. The Passacaglia has an organic flow and good characterization, though at 16’21” it lacks the driving momentum found in the faster performances by the composer (Polish RSO/Warner Classics); Tortelier (BBC Philharmonic/Chandos); and Dohnányi (Cleveland SO/Decca). The compositional style of the Cello Concerto (1970) is entirely different, the writing far more dissonant (including the use of quarter tones) and contrapuntal. It also features Lutosławski’s aleatoric (sometimes referred to as ‘controlled chaos’) technique. From its inception, the composer claimed it was pure, abstract music, but this has not stopped people (including Rostropovich) from suggesting that the almost constant strife between soloist and orchestra represents the individual’s struggle for freedom within an oppressive political system (a situation which both musicians experienced). The Introduction opens with the soloist’s personal musings around a repeated D, but conflict begins when the cello is chastised by angry trumpets. I must acknowledge that I connect with this music more readily through the unauthorized program; as abstract art, it is less compelling. Rostropovich’s recording, with the Orchestre de Paris conducted by the composer, is an obvious reference performance against which every subsequent release is compared. It is not that every soloist must match Rostropovich’s ‘larger than life’ persona, but there must be a palpable connection with and commitment to this difficult music. I find that in three other readings: Pieter Wispelwey (Netherlands RPO/van Steen/Channel Classics), Paul Watkins (BBC SO/Gardner/Chandos), and Andrzej Bauer (Polish NRSO/Wit/Naxos). Gustavo Gimeno. Photo © Anne Dokter. Wispelwey is especially good at capturing the music’s shifts in atmosphere, and his gorgeous playing in the Cantilena even outshines Rostropovich. Queyras’s technique is beyond reproach, and his reading has plenty of character (as do the orchestra and conductor). Nevertheless, the reading is not as uniquely compelling as those others listed, and both Wit and Gardner inspire greater drama and character from their orchestras. Ernest Bloch‘s Schelomo is based on music originally intended for King Solomon in an unfinished opera, Jezabel. Nicholas Reyland’s liner notes tell us that the cellist Alexandre Barjansky convinced Bloch the cello “could convey Solomon’s meditations ‘just as expressively, if less specifically,’ freeing the depiction from language.” This is sumptuous, emotionally extroverted music. Rostropovich’s reading with Bernstein and the Orchestre National de France (Warner Classics) is considered a classic recording, though I find Bernstein’s effort to wring every ounce of emotion from the performance draws attention away from the music. My favorite performance (also on Warner) features Steven Isserlis, accompanied by the London SO under Richard Hickox. Queyras’ reading is similarly moving, if more inward looking than Isserlis or Sol Gabetta (Orchestre National de Lyon/Slatkin/Sony Classical), and Gimeno ensures that the complexity and richness of the orchestral part is more than mere accompaniment. In short, these are exceptionally fine performances, which nonetheless fail to displace current frontrunners. Home » Jazz Articles » Album Review » Matt White: Matt White's Dolly

 LIKE 4
Matt White: Matt White's Dolly
By Katchie Cartwright
May 25, 2026
View read count
A miniature doll-like effigy of the great country music singer-songwriter Dolly Parton adorns the cover of trumpeter-composer Matt White's Dolly. How did the Queen of Country become the subject of this fascinating (if awkwardly-branded) mainstream jazz album? Happenstance.

White was researching Gullah songs for his 2023 album, Lowcountry (Ropeadope), when YouTube "Pandorized" him into a video of a young Parton, guitar in hand, performing "The Bridge," solo, on the Porter Wagoner television show in the '60s. He made a rhythmic connection, and—voilà—the seed was planted.

Working with Liz Kelley, the project's excellent vocalist, White created a little dogma for himself, a set of arranging rules: Keep the vocal melodies and lyrics the same, keep the original keys and all the modulations. "Everything else was open to change." Kelley serves as a solid stand-in for Parton. Her singing style is country—with the requisite cry and twang—but she manages to avoid imitation, coming across as genuine. White has her holding down the melodic fort sans improvisation, which (ties her up you might say, but) frees the band to respond to Parton's songs in a jazz milieu without altering their most recognizeable feature, the vocal line.

The settings are engaging and complex, full of jazz harmonies, melodies and rhythms. And the instrumentalists are superb players and improvisers. Their lines swirl around the vocal ones, alternately in call-and-response fashion, contrapuntally, via ostinatos, in fills and instrumental breaks, and through solo statements.

Between heartwrenching songs of "bad men and birds" (as Kelley put it) written by a very young Parton, "9 to 5" appears in three riveting instrumental settings that feature the powerful rhythm team of Demetrius Doctor on organ and Colleen Clark on drums, preaching the gospel of a hard day's work in brief two-to-three-minute sermons (with fairly equal parts gravity, levity, and liberty). You might even sense a bit of Bud Powell's "Parisian Thoroughfare" (Clifford Brown & Max Roach, Capitol, 1954).

As invigorating and beautifully-performed as the vocal arrangments are, the three instrumental versions of "9 to 5," interspersed throughout the program, stop the show with their freedom and abstraction.

Throughout, the sound of the band is striking. On top are Kelley's vocal eloquence and the fleet grace of White's cornet (he bought one for the occasion), along with Tim Fischer's lyrical guitar. On the bottom, Doctor's prodigious organ and Clark's sizzling, crackling drums, which sometimes walk the line between jazz and country idioms. This is an unusual album without a doubt, one worth more than just a few spins.
Track Listing

Down from Dover; My Blue Tears; 9 to 5 (1); The Bridge; 9 to 5 (2); The Carroll County Accident; 9 to 5 (3); Jolene; Little Bird.

items.body:
EXPLORE  SEARCH JAZZ NEAR YOU
